UNIT.subject: Biology
UNIT.strand: Strand 3.0: Anatomy and Physiology of Animals
UNIT.substrand: Sub-Strand 3.2: Growth and Development in Animals
UNIT.content:
• Metamorphosis (complete and incomplete metamorphosis in insects)
• Role of growth hormones in insects
• Growth curves in animals (continuous and intermittent growth)
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) distinguish between complete and incomplete metamorphosis in insects,
b) describe the role of hormones in growth and development in insects,
c) analyse growth curves in animals,
d) appreciate the importance of growth and development in animals.
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Digital Literacy: The learner appropriately selects animations illustrating the effect of hormones on insect growth and development (Lesson 5).
• Creativity and Imagination: The learner adjusts and rethinks their ideas while modelling life cycles of different insects (Lessons 1 and 6).
• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: The learner analyses growth curves and calculates growth rates at different growth phases on sigmoid and intermittent curves (Lessons 2 and 3).
UNIT.values:
• Love: The learner handles insects with compassion as they collect data on animals to calculate growth rates at different growth phases (Lesson 1).
• Unity: The learner collaborates with others while plotting graphs to illustrate complete and incomplete metamorphosis in insects (Lessons 2 and 3).
UNIT.sep:
• Developing and Using Models: Students build and revise life cycle models of grasshoppers (incomplete) and houseflies (complete) from Lesson 1 to Lesson 6.
• Analyzing and Interpreting Data: Students plot and interpret intermittent and sigmoid growth curves and calculate growth rates (Lessons 2 and 3).
• Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information: Students research insect hormones and evaluate animations and flowcharts (Lessons 4 and 5).
• Engaging in Argument from Evidence: Students build Claim-Evidence-Reasoning posters answering the Driving Question (Lesson 6).
UNIT.pcis:
• Animal Welfare: The learner treats animals with care while collecting data for plotting growth curves in animals (Lessons 1 and 2).
• Good Governance: The learner demonstrates principles of leadership while working with peers to search for information on insect hormones and their roles in growth and development (Lesson 4).
UNIT.careers:
• Agricultural Entomologists: study insect life stages to time interventions on pests such as locusts and armyworms in Kenyan farms.
• Veterinary Researchers: use growth curves to monitor the health and development of livestock.
• Parasitologists: study the life cycles and hormonal control of vectors such as mosquitoes and tsetse flies.
• Wildlife Biologists: track growth and development of wild animals in places like the Rift Valley and Maasai Mara.
• Horticultural Pest Control Specialists: design pest control that targets insect hormones in flower and vegetable farms around Naivasha.
UNIT.focus: This unit uses the puzzle of an empty insect skin beside a larger, newly emerged insect to drive inquiry into how animals grow. Students move from observing life cycles to plotting growth curves, then to the hormones that control moulting and metamorphosis. They keep a Driving Question Board and revise a cumulative model each lesson, using low-cost local specimens and printable data sheets.
UNIT.phenomenon: On a maize leaf or tree bark in a school garden, students find a crunchy, empty, perfectly shaped insect skin (exuvia) with a split down its back, hanging beside a newly emerged grasshopper or cicada that is clearly larger than the skin it just left. Alongside it are photos or samples of caterpillars that become motionless pupae and later emerge as butterflies. This is puzzling: how can an animal grow bigger than a hard shell it was wearing, why does it not grow smoothly, and why do some insects change shape completely while others look like small adults? Students often think insects peel like sunburned skin or that caterpillars simply melt and rebuild without control.
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• Locust nymphs in the Rift Valley and northern Kenya gradually gain wings across stages, while housefly maggots look nothing like adult flies.
• Maize farmers see armyworm caterpillars feeding heavily and then vanishing into pupae in the soil before moths emerge.
• A graph of a calf's or chick's mass over time forms a smooth S-shape, unlike the staircase pattern of a grasshopper's length.
• Pesticides used on Kenyan farms can stop insect pests from moulting properly, which links to hormone control.
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: How does an animal outgrow its own hard shell, and why do some animals radically change shape while others just grow bigger?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTIONS:
1. How does growth in animals occur?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1: Insects follow two distinct developmental pathways: complete metamorphosis (4 stages) vs. incomplete metamorphosis (3 stages). | Observe live specimens/specimen cards (grasshopper nymphs vs. housefly larvae/pupae); sort them into developmental sequences; construct initial comparative models. | Preserved insect specimens, hand lenses, life cycle diagram cards. | Why do grasshoppers increase in length in sudden jumps rather than smooth, daily growth?
Lesson 2: Animals with exoskeletons exhibit intermittent (stepwise) growth curves because moulting (ecdysis) must occur before body dimensions increase. | Collect measurement data from insect nymph stages; plot length/mass vs. time to construct intermittent growth curves. | Measurement rulers, insect growth dataset worksheets, graph paper. | How do non-exoskeletal animals or organisms with internal skeletons grow compared to insects?
Lesson 3: Vertebrates and soft-bodied animals exhibit continuous growth represented by a sigmoid (S-shaped) curve with distinct growth phases. | Plot mass/height data over time for mammals/birds; calculate growth rates across lag, exponential, deceleration, and stationary phases. | Animal growth rate data tables, graph paper, calculators. | What triggers and controls the precise timing of moulting and metamorphosis in insects?
Lesson 4: Specific hormones (e.g., Ecdysone, Juvenile Hormone, Brain Hormone) interact to regulate moulting and stage transitions in insect life cycles. | Search information on insect hormones; analyze experimental flowcharts showing hormone gland removal/injection effects in larvae. | Reference texts, hormone function flowcharts, digital research devices. | Can visual animations help us see how hormone concentration balances dictate larva-to-pupa shifts?
Lesson 5: Fluctuations in Juvenile Hormone levels dictate whether an insect moults into another nymph/larva or transitions into a pupa/adult. | Select and view digital animations showing hormonal regulation in insect metamorphosis; synthesize findings into interactive flow diagrams. | Digital devices/projector, insect development animation links, flow chart templates. | How do all these growth patterns and chemical controls ensure animal survival and species continuity?
Lesson 6: Controlled growth and developmental transitions allow animals to optimize resource use, reduce parent-offspring competition, and survive harsh environments. | Revisit and refine initial Day 1 models; construct Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) posters answering the main Driving Question. | Chart paper, markers, DQB sticky notes, CER template. | Unit complete — How might human pesticides disrupt these exact hormonal pathways in agricultural pests?

LESSONS.title: The Empty Skin on the Maize Leaf: Two Ways Insects Grow
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 3.2: Growth and Development in Animals
LESSONS.aresKeywords: exuvia, moulting, ecdysis, exoskeleton, nymph, larva, pupa, adult, complete metamorphosis, incomplete metamorphosis, grasshopper, housefly, Driving Question Board

slo.purpose: To launch the anchoring phenomenon (an empty insect skin beside a larger, newly emerged insect) and to have learners discover through evidence that insects follow two distinct developmental pathways: complete metamorphosis (4 stages) and incomplete metamorphosis (3 stages).
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to distinguish between complete metamorphosis (egg, larva, pupa, adult) and incomplete metamorphosis (egg, nymph, adult) using specimens and life cycle cards (SLO a: distinguish between complete and incomplete metamorphosis in insects).
slo.skills: Predicting, observing and recording with a hand lens, sorting specimens into developmental sequences, constructing initial comparative models (NGSS SEP: Developing and Using Models), asking questions (NGSS SEP: Asking Questions), and stating a first Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (NGSS SEP: Engaging in Argument from Evidence).
slo.attitudes: Core competency: Creativity and Imagination - the learner adjusts and rethinks their ideas while modelling life cycles of different insects. Value: Love - the learner handles insects with compassion. Value: Unity - learners collaborate in sorting and modelling. PCI: Animal Welfare - the learner treats animals with care.
slo.keyInquiry: How does growth in animals occur?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This lesson opens the unit by presenting the puzzle of the empty exuvia and the larger insect beside it. Learners establish the two developmental pathways as a foundation, surface their ideas (such as 'insects peel like sunburn' or 'caterpillars melt and rebuild'), and open the DQB. The new question it raises for Lesson 2 is: Why do grasshoppers increase in length in sudden jumps rather than smooth, daily growth?
slo.safetyNotes: Animal welfare: collect insects only from the school garden or compound by hand or soft net, take only the minimum needed (about 2 to 3 per group), never kill, pin or injure live insects for this lesson, and use preserved specimens only from already-dead or ethically sourced material. Keep live insects in ventilated containers (jars with perforated lids, a leaf and a damp cotton wool piece) in shade, and return them to where they were found within the same day. Handle gently with clean dry hands or a soft brush, and wash hands with soap afterwards. Do not handle insects if you have allergies; use hand lenses and avoid contact with eyes. Wear gloves for preserved specimens (preservative may irritate), keep jars closed, and avoid tasting or sniffing. Do not collect wasps, bees, hairy caterpillars or any insect that stings or irritates. Where internet is limited, use the printed data sheets and cards.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin in the school garden or at a display table with a real exuvia (a split, crunchy skin from a grasshopper or cicada on a maize leaf) beside a larger insect. They predict how the insect got bigger than its skin, draw a before-and-after diagram, observe preserved specimens and live grasshopper nymphs and housefly larvae/pupae with hand lenses, sort specimen and life cycle cards into sequences, and compare the two pathways in a model. A Gallery Walk lets peers review the models, and learners post questions on a new DQB. They leave with a first CER claim and the question: why do grasshoppers grow in sudden jumps rather than smoothly?

framework.learnerExperience: Learners gather around a display (or the school garden maize plants) showing an empty exuvia with a split down its back next to a larger grasshopper nymph or adult, plus photos of a caterpillar, a motionless pupa and a butterfly emerging. Individually (3 min) they draw a two-stage before-and-after diagram of how the insect grew, annotating where they think the old shell went and what happened inside it. Then Think-Pair-Share: they compare drawings with a partner and write one prediction: 'I predict the insect got bigger than its skin because...'. Common ideas are recorded, such as 'it peels like sunburned skin' or 'the caterpillar melts and rebuilds'.
framework.teacherMoves: Hold up the exuvia and say: 'This was alive this morning, hanging on a maize leaf in our school garden. Look closely. The skin is smaller than the insect beside it. What do you notice? What do you wonder?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds in silence before taking any answer. Say: 'Draw first, talk second. There are no wrong ideas today; I want to see your real thinking.' During pair talk, circulate and listen for the 'peeling like sunburn' and 'melting caterpillar' ideas without correcting. Cold-call 4 pairs (not volunteers) with: 'Tell us what your partner predicted, not what you predicted.' Record 4-5 ideas on the board using learners' own words. Say: 'Keep your drawing; we will revisit it at the end of the lesson.' Remind learners about gentle handling: 'These are living things; we handle them with compassion.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) and Think-Pair-Share: Drawing a prediction before instruction makes learners commit to an idea, so later evidence creates a genuine 'need to know'. Pair sharing lets every learner rehearse their idea, and explaining a partner's idea builds listening and exposes the range of misconceptions that the class will test.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe and note on a class checklist: (1) Does the drawing show two stages with the old shell placed somewhere (e.g., 'dried up', 'peeled off', 'left behind')? (2) Does the learner show the insect inside the skin, or a skin that stretches or shrinks? (3) Does the learner use words like 'melt', 'peel' or 'stretch'? Tally the number of learners who hold the 'peeling' or 'melting' idea. Keep drawings in the learner portfolio as the baseline model.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4 (assigned roles: handler, recorder, sorter, reporter) learners rotate through the evidence stations using hand lenses: Station 1: live grasshopper nymphs (or specimen cards) of different sizes plus an exuvia; Station 2: housefly larvae (maggot), pupae (puparia) and adults (preserved specimens or cards); Station 3: butterfly/caterpillar and pupa photo cards (e.g., cabbage white butterfly on sukuma wiki). At each station they sketch what they see, record features on a print-based data sheet (body shape, wings present or absent, legs, mobility, feeding, size), and note whether the young look like small adults. Then they sort the life cycle diagram cards into two developmental sequences: Sequence A (egg, nymph, nymph, adult) for grasshopper and Sequence B (egg, larva, pupa, adult) for housefly. They count the number of stages in each.
framework.teacherMoves: Before distribution say: 'Insects are living animals. Hands clean, movements slow, and every insect returns to the garden today.' Check that jars are in the shade and lids have holes. Say: 'Use your hand lens 2 cm from the specimen. Describe what you see, not what you think it should be.' Circulate with prompts: 'Does this young grasshopper look like the adult? What is different? What is the same?', 'Where are the wings on the maggot? On the pupa?', 'What do you see on the exuvia that you can also see on the live insect, such as eyes, leg joints or mouthparts?' After each prompt give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before moving on. Cold-call 3 groups to share one surprising observation. If a group sorts incorrectly, do not correct; ask: 'What evidence made you put this card here?' Ensure all insects are gently returned or kept in the shade, and collect preserved specimens afterward.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (Observe step): Direct comparison of real specimens gives learners first-hand evidence about stage number and body shape. Sorting cards into sequences forces them to apply criteria (does the young look like the adult? is there a resting stage?), moving from description to pattern recognition.
framework.formativeAssessment: Oral probes at each station: 'How do you know this is the same animal at a different stage?' Look for observable indicators: learner uses the hand lens correctly; the data sheet records at least 3 differing features between larva and adult; the grasshopper sequence has no pupa and the housefly sequence has a pupa; the learner states 'nymphs look like small adults' or 'larvae look nothing like adults'. Record on the checklist which groups sorted correctly first time and which need support.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups build an initial comparative model on a large sheet or manila paper: two columns (grasshopper: incomplete metamorphosis; housefly: complete metamorphosis) showing the stages in order with labelled drawings, and arrows showing where the exuvia (old skin) is left. They add a short caption: 'What changes? What stays the same?' Then they write a first Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) statement: Claim: 'Insects follow two developmental pathways.' Evidence: observations from the specimens and cards (e.g., 'the housefly has a motionless pupa stage but the grasshopper does not'). Reasoning: why the evidence supports the claim. They then revisit their original Predict drawing and mark in a different colour anything they would now change. Finally, each group prepares to present.
framework.teacherMoves: Model one CER example on the board using a different Kenyan insect: 'Claim: A mosquito from Lake Victoria shores follows complete metamorphosis. Evidence: its young is a wriggler in water and it has a pupa. Reasoning: ...' Say: 'Notice I did not say "I think". I used evidence.' Give sentence frames: 'I observed...', 'This shows...', 'Therefore...'. Circulate and ask: 'Why do you think the grasshopper nymph has no pupa stage?', 'What does the arrow to the exuvia mean in your model?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 3 groups to state their CER aloud (not volunteers). Address the misconception gently: 'Some of you drew the old skin peeling like sunburn. Look at the exuvia again: what do you notice about the split on its back?' Do not give the full explanation; say: 'We have a puzzle: the insect is bigger than its skin. How? That is for our next lessons.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) modelling: Explicit modelling by the teacher shows learners how to link observations to a conclusion, building scientific argumentation. Building a comparative model makes thinking visible and gives a testable representation that will be revised in later lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check each group's model against a quick rubric: (1) Grasshopper shows 3 stages and no pupa; (2) Housefly shows 4 stages including pupa; (3) Exuvia is shown; (4) CER has a claim, at least one observation as evidence, and a reason. Oral probe: 'Which part of your evidence best supports your claim?' Note groups using 'I think' instead of evidence for follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners display the phenomenon images and the driving question in the centre of a chart or wall space: 'How does an animal outgrow its own hard shell, and why do some animals radically change shape while others just grow bigger?' Individually, they write 2 questions on sticky notes or slips of paper (one about the shell, one about the shape change). In groups they cluster questions into categories (e.g., How does the shell split? What controls growth? What happens inside the pupa? Why do some insects not have a pupa?). Then they take part in a Gallery Walk: groups walk around to view other groups' models and DQB clusters, leaving one 'star' (a strength) and one 'wonder' (a question) on sticky notes.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'A good question starts with how or why, and cannot be answered with yes or no.' Model: 'Who can turn "Does the skin break?" into a how or why question?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 5 learners to place a question on the DQB and explain where it fits. Highlight the question 'Why does the grasshopper get bigger suddenly rather than gradually?' if it arises, or introduce it yourself: 'I noticed that the smallest nymph and the next one are very different in size, but there is nothing in between. Why might that be?' During the Gallery Walk, give 6 minutes with a signal to rotate every 2 minutes. Say: 'Be kind, be specific, and use evidence in your feedback.' Circulate and note questions that link to later lessons (hormones, growth curves).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Gallery Walk and DQB: Peer review of models exposes learners to alternative ideas and strengthens critique skills. The DQB gives learners ownership of the inquiry and keeps the puzzle visible, so that each later lesson answers learner-generated questions.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a peer rubric during the Gallery Walk with 3 criteria: stages in correct order, evidence shown, clear labels. Look for observable indicators: at least 80% of learners post two questions; questions are 'how/why' types; stars and wonders reference specific features (e.g., 'You showed the pupa clearly'). Sort questions into themes to plan Lessons 2-6.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to their original Predict drawing and, using a different colour, revise it to show what they now think about the insect and its old skin, noting what they are still unsure of (e.g., 'How did the insect get out? Why is the new insect bigger?'). Then they complete an exit ticket: (1) Name the stages for the grasshopper and the housefly. (2) Which pathway has a pupa? (3) One question you still have about how the insect got bigger than its skin. They add the first entry to the class Summary Table (What we observed / What we learned / What we can explain so far).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take out your first drawing. With a different coloured pen, change anything you now think is different. It is fine to keep ideas that you still believe.' Allow 3 minutes of silent work. Cold-call 3 learners to share one revision: 'What did you change and what evidence made you change it?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Then pose the bridging question: 'We know the stages. But why does the grasshopper grow in sudden jumps instead of a little each day? We will test that next lesson.' Collect exit tickets at the door. Remind learners to return live insects to the garden gently and wash hands with soap. Say: 'Bring any empty insect skins you find at home or in the shamba tomorrow.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision with exit ticket: Revising the initial model in a different colour makes learning visible and shows learners how their thinking has changed with evidence. The bridging question links this lesson to the next (growth in sudden steps), keeping the storyline coherent.
framework.formativeAssessment: Exit ticket check: (1) correct stage lists for both insects; (2) pupa linked to complete metamorphosis; (3) a genuine question about growth or the shell. Observable indicators for the revised drawing: uses a second colour, adds at least one change based on evidence, and identifies one remaining uncertainty. Sort tickets into 'secure', 'partly secure' and 'needs support' groups and plan short re-teaching at the start of Lesson 2.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners still held the 'peeling like sunburn' or 'caterpillar melts' ideas after the Observe phase, and what evidence did they cite? Did every group handle live insects with care and return them safely? Which questions on the DQB can anchor Lessons 2 to 4 (shell and moulting, hormones, growth curves)? Did learners without internet access use the printed data sheets and cards effectively? What would I change about group roles, wait time or the sequencing of stations next time?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed an empty insect skin (exuvia) with a split on its back beside a larger insect; grasshopper nymphs that look like small adults with no pupa; housefly larvae that look nothing like the adult and a motionless pupa stage.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Insects follow two developmental pathways: incomplete metamorphosis (egg, nymph, adult: 3 stages) as in the grasshopper, and complete metamorphosis (egg, larva, pupa, adult: 4 stages) as in the housefly and butterfly.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can explain that the two pathways differ in the number of stages and in whether the young resemble the adult, but we cannot yet explain how the insect got bigger than its old skin or why grasshoppers grow in sudden jumps rather than smoothly.

LESSONS.title: Stepwise Growth: Why Hard-Shelled Animals Grow in Jumps
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 3.2: Growth and Development in Animals
LESSONS.aresKeywords: exoskeleton, moulting, ecdysis, exuvia, nymph, instar, intermittent growth, growth curve, incomplete metamorphosis, hormone

slo.purpose: Learners collect and plot length and mass data from insect nymph stages to construct intermittent (stepwise) growth curves, and explain that moulting (ecdysis) must occur before body dimensions can increase in animals with exoskeletons.
slo.knowledge: a) distinguish between complete and incomplete metamorphosis (early foundation); c) analyse growth curves in animals (intermittent growth). Learners explain that a rigid exoskeleton limits size, so length increases only after ecdysis, giving a staircase-shaped curve with plateaus (intermoult periods) and sudden rises (moulting).
slo.skills: Collecting measurement data (length, mass) from datasets and, where possible, live specimens; plotting line graphs on graph paper; interpreting growth curves; constructing claims supported by evidence and reasoning (CER); NGSS practices: Analyzing and Interpreting Data, Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking, Constructing Explanations.
slo.attitudes: Love: handle insects with compassion while collecting data. Unity: collaborate with peers while plotting and comparing graphs. Appreciation of the importance of growth and development in animals. Digital Literacy and Creativity and Imagination are supported as learners select and rethink their models. Animal Welfare (PCI): treat animals with care. Good governance (PCI): demonstrate leadership in group roles.
slo.keyInquiry: How does growth in animals occur?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 gave learners the phenomenon: an empty exuvia beside a larger newly emerged grasshopper, and caterpillars becoming pupae. Learners wondered how an animal can outgrow a hard shell. Lesson 2 gives the first quantitative evidence: growth in nymphs is stepwise, not smooth. This explains why the animal is bigger than its shell (it swelled and expanded after splitting the old skin) and sets up Lesson 3 (growth rate calculations with standard formulas) and the new question: How do non-exoskeletal animals or organisms with internal skeletons grow compared to insects?
slo.safetyNotes: Animal welfare first: collect only a few insects (e.g., 3-5 grasshoppers or nymphs per class) from the school garden using soft containers or hands, never crushing them. Provide ventilated containers with maize leaves and sukuma wiki leaves, keep them shaded, and never hold them longer than 10 minutes. Measure with a ruler by gently placing the insect in a clear container or measure exuviae/photos instead of handling. Release every insect at the exact collection site the same day. Do not collect protected, stinging or biting species (wasps, bees, driver ants); avoid venomous insects. Wash hands after handling. Where specimens are unavailable or internet is limited, use the printed dataset worksheets. Follow national animal welfare standards: no harm, no killing, minimal handling, and prompt release. Learners with allergies should record data rather than handle.

LESSONS.overview: Learners return to the school garden phenomenon: a grasshopper emerges larger than the hard exuvia it left on a maize leaf. They first predict what a graph of a nymph's length over time would look like (smooth line or steps?). They then measure real or dataset-based nymph lengths and masses (such as a locust or grasshopper nymph from Kisumu or Rift Valley farms) with rulers, plot them on graph paper, and observe plateaus and sudden jumps. Using CER, they explain that the exoskeleton cannot stretch, so the animal grows only right after moulting while the new cuticle is soft. A gallery walk allows peer review. The Driving Question Board is updated with new questions about internal skeleton animals, and the class revises its model of how an insect gets bigger than its shell.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners view the exuvia and emerged grasshopper from the school garden (specimen or photo). Individually they sketch on graph paper axes what they think the graph of a nymph's body length against time looks like over 10 weeks (smooth curve, straight line, or steps), and write one sentence explaining why, linking to how the animal became bigger than its shell. They use Think-Pair-Share to compare predictions and record a pair prediction on a sticky note.
framework.teacherMoves: Hold up the exuvia: "Last lesson we found this empty skin next to a bigger grasshopper. If we measured this grasshopper every few days from hatching, what would its growth graph look like?" Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds in silence before anyone writes. Allow 2 minutes for individual sketching, 3 minutes for pairing. Then cold-call 4 pairs, ensuring at least 2 different shapes are shared. Ask: "What in your idea of the shell made you draw it that way?" Record all predictions on the board without judging. Remind learners of animal welfare rules for later handling.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) and Think-Pair-Share: committing to a prediction first exposes the common misconception that growth is smooth, like a child's height, creating cognitive conflict when real data shows steps. Pair talk lets every learner voice reasoning before the class discussion.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether sketches show smooth lines versus steps; tally on a checklist how many learners link the shell to growth limits. Look for: (1) a labelled graph with axes, (2) a written reason. Use the tally to decide how much scaffolding to give during plotting.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4 with defined roles (measurer, recorder, plotter, welfare officer), learners collect data. Where live nymphs from the school garden are available, they gently place them in a clear container over a ruler, and measure length (mm) and, if a balance is available, mass (g) for each instar; otherwise they work with the printed insect growth dataset worksheet (e.g., desert locust nymph lengths over 35 days with moulting dates in Rift Valley/Turkana conditions). They plot length against time on graph paper, join points, and mark the days when moulting occurred. They then describe the shape: plateaus and sudden rises. They also plot mass for comparison and note that mass may increase more gradually between moults while length jumps.
framework.teacherMoves: Model one data point on the board: "Day 10, length 12 mm. Where does it go on the axes?" Circulate and ask oral probes: "What is happening to the length between Day 12 and Day 18?" and "Why might the length not change even though the insect keeps eating sukuma wiki?" Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each probe. Cold-call 3 groups to report the day of a moult. Check the welfare officer is enforcing gentle handling and a 10-minute limit. Provide print-based sheets for groups lacking specimens. Do not give the explanation yet; prompt: "Mark where the graph jumps."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (observe step): learners generate the pattern themselves from data, so the staircase shape is evidence they discovered, not a fact they were told. Graphing converts numbers into a visual pattern that can be compared with their prediction.
framework.formativeAssessment: Growth curve graph check: use a checklist at each group: correct axes labels with units, even scale, all points plotted accurately, moulting days marked, line shows plateaus and rises. Oral probes during modelling record whether learners can point to a plateau and a jump. Note groups needing help with scale.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners use Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) to answer: Why does the nymph's length increase in steps? The teacher models one CER on the board; groups then write their own on a CER template. Claim: growth in animals with exoskeletons is intermittent. Evidence: specific data from their graph (e.g., length stayed at 14 mm from Day 12-17, then jumped to 19 mm on Day 18). Reasoning: the hard, non-stretching exoskeleton limits size, so the animal must moult (ecdysis), split the old cuticle (leaving the exuvia), and swell while the new cuticle is soft before it hardens. They then do a Gallery Walk, posting graphs and CERs, and use a peer rubric to leave two stars and one wish on each.
framework.teacherMoves: Model: "My claim is... my evidence is Day 18... my reasoning connects to the exuvia on the maize leaf." Ask: "How does this explain why the grasshopper is bigger than its shell?" WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to give reasoning aloud, then 2 to challenge or add. Address the misconception that insects peel like sunburned skin: "Is the exuvia a thin peel, or a complete hard casing with legs and eyes covers?" During the Gallery Walk (8 minutes, rotating every 2 minutes), ask: "Which graph gives the strongest evidence, and why?" Briefly introduce that hormones (ecdysone) trigger moulting, to be explored later, and that growth rate calculations come in Lesson 3.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) modelling and Gallery Walks: CER forces learners to tie their claims to specific data and a scientific mechanism, while peer review exposes them to alternative graphs and strengthens argumentation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Peer rubric during the gallery walk: criteria are claim stated clearly, evidence quotes data with numbers and units, reasoning links exoskeleton and ecdysis. Check that at least 80% of CERs mention the non-stretching exoskeleton and moulting before growth. Exit ticket: "Draw a stepwise curve and label where moulting occurs; explain in one sentence why the insect is larger than its exuvia."

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the class DQB with the driving question about outgrowing a hard shell and why some animals change shape while others just get bigger. On sticky notes they add (a) what they now know (e.g., growth is stepwise, moulting comes first) and (b) new questions, such as: How do animals with internal bones like goats, cattle or humans in Kenya grow? Is their growth also in steps? What triggers moulting? Why do butterflies have a pupa stage? They place notes under categories such as Answered, Partly Answered and New.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Look at our board. Which questions did today's graphs help us answer, and which new ones did they raise?" Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before sharing. Cold-call 4 learners to place and justify a note. Highlight the planned question: "How do non-exoskeletal animals or organisms with internal skeletons grow compared to insects?" and invite learners to predict for next lesson. Move answered notes to the answered column with evidence from the graphs.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with Think-Pair-Share: learners see their learning progress and generate the next investigation questions, building ownership and a coherent storyline from lesson to lesson.
framework.formativeAssessment: Review the quality of new questions: look for those that are testable and linked to today's evidence. Count how many learners contribute a question and how many link to the phenomenon. Use the notes to plan Lesson 3.

framework.learnerExperience: In their groups, learners revise their model from Lesson 1 by drawing a labelled diagram sequence of a grasshopper nymph: the nymph inside a tight exoskeleton, the old cuticle splitting along the back, the insect expanding with a soft new cuticle, and the hardening of the new cuticle. Beside it they paste a small version of their stepwise graph, linking each plateau and jump to a stage in the diagram. They add one sentence on why the emerged grasshopper is larger than the exuvia. They list what they still cannot explain (the shape change in butterflies; hormone control). Groups present a 1-minute oral explanation, and peers use rubrics.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Show me where on your model the growth actually happens, and where the graph shows it." Circulate and ask oral probes: "What would happen to the nymph if it could not moult?" WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 groups to present, then ask 2 other learners to restate the key idea. Encourage creativity and rethinking of ideas. Close with the exit ticket and hand-out of the print dataset for Lesson 3 growth-rate calculations. Remind learners to release any held insects at the original site and wash hands.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model building with peer review: learners integrate graph evidence with the mechanism of ecdysis into a visual model, which makes their thinking visible and revisable. Peer rubrics encourage collaborative critique (Unity).
framework.formativeAssessment: Peer rubric during presentations: model includes (1) exoskeleton labelled, (2) moulting and exuvia, (3) expansion before hardening, (4) link to graph steps. Oral probes record whether learners can explain why growth occurs only after moulting. Exit ticket collected and sorted into ready, nearly ready and needs support.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners still believed growth in insects is smooth or that the exuvia is just peeled skin after the graph work? Did every group handle insects gently and release them? Were the print datasets sufficient where specimens were unavailable? Which CER components (evidence with numbers, reasoning about the exoskeleton) were weakest, and how will you address them before Lesson 3 growth-rate calculations? What new questions on the DQB can seed the comparison with animals with internal skeletons?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We measured and plotted the length and mass of insect nymphs over time and saw that the graph rose in steps: flat periods with no length change, followed by sudden jumps when the insect moulted, leaving an empty exuvia.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Animals with a hard exoskeleton cannot grow smoothly because the shell does not stretch. They must moult (ecdysis) first, then swell while the new cuticle is soft, giving an intermittent (stepwise) growth curve.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The grasshopper on the maize leaf is bigger than its exuvia because it split the old shell, expanded its body before the new cuticle hardened, and so grew in a sudden jump. New question: how do animals with internal skeletons grow compared to insects?

LESSONS.title: Growth Curves: Why Do Vertebrates and Soft-Bodied Animals Grow Smoothly in an S-Shape While Insects with Hard Shells Grow in Steps?
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 3.2: Growth and Development in Animals
LESSONS.aresKeywords: sigmoid growth curve, continuous growth, lag phase, exponential phase, deceleration phase, stationary phase, growth rate, intermittent growth, exuvia, Kenyan data

slo.purpose: Students gather quantitative evidence that vertebrates and soft-bodied animals grow continuously, giving an S-shaped (sigmoid) curve with four phases, and contrast this with the stepwise growth of the moulting insect in our phenomenon.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: (a) analyse growth curves in animals (continuous and intermittent); (b) describe the lag, exponential (log), deceleration and stationary phases of a sigmoid curve; (c) calculate growth rate using Growth rate = (final value - initial value) / time interval.
slo.skills: NGSS SEP: Analysing and Interpreting Data (plot mass/height against time, identify trends); Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking (calculate growth rates with standard formulas); Constructing Explanations (CER). Learners collect, plot and interpret height, length or mass data and calculate growth rates at different growth phases.
slo.attitudes: Core competencies: Digital Literacy (selecting suitable data sources or animations when available) and Creativity and Imagination (adjusting and rethinking ideas when revising models). Values: Love (handling any live animals with compassion while collecting data) and Unity (collaborating while plotting graphs). PCIs: Animal Welfare (treating animals with care when collecting data for growth curves) and Good Governance (demonstrating leadership roles in groups). Appreciate the importance of growth and development in animals.
slo.keyInquiry: How does growth in animals occur?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 1-2 learners saw the empty exuvia beside a larger grasshopper and learned that a hard exoskeleton forces growth in steps (intermittent growth). Lesson 3 adds the contrast case: animals without a rigid outer shell, such as Kenyan chicks, calves, goats and humans, grow continuously in a sigmoid curve. Learners calculate growth rates to show that growth is not random but has phases. This sets up the new question for Lesson 4: What triggers and controls the precise timing of moulting and metamorphosis in insects?
slo.safetyNotes: Mostly desk-based data analysis, so low risk. If any live insects (for example grasshoppers from the school garden) are shown as a comparison, collect only a few using hands or soft containers, handle gently, keep in ventilated containers with maize leaves, do not harm or squeeze them, avoid hot sun, wash hands afterwards, and release them at the exact place of collection at the end of the lesson in line with national animal welfare standards. Do not collect from protected areas. Calculators and graph paper only; no sharp tools needed. Data sheets are printed so no internet is required.

LESSONS.overview: Learners return to the exuvia phenomenon and ask: if the grasshopper grows in sudden jumps because of its hard shell, how do animals without such a shell, such as a Kenyan broiler chick from Kiambu, a Friesian calf from Nyahururu or a human child, grow? Learners first predict the shape of a mass-against-time graph. They then plot printed data tables (chick mass over 10 weeks, calf mass over 2 years, a child's height over 20 years, and a comparison grasshopper nymph length with stepped moult data), calculate growth rates for each phase using Growth rate = (final - initial) / time, and identify lag, exponential, deceleration and stationary phases. They use CER to explain why the vertebrate curve is smooth while the insect curve is a staircase, add to the Driving Question Board, and revise their class model. The lesson ends with the question: what controls when an insect moults?

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) Learners look at the phenomenon photo again: the exuvia beside the bigger grasshopper. The teacher asks: 'The grasshopper grew in jumps. What would a graph of a Kenyan broiler chick's mass over 10 weeks look like?' Individually, learners sketch a prediction on a blank axis (mass on y, weeks on x) and write one sentence: 'I think the graph will look like ___ because ___.' They then Think-Pair-Share and compare sketches with a partner, noting whether the line is straight, stepped, or curved. Learners also predict: Does a chick have an exuvia like the grasshopper?
framework.teacherMoves: Display the exuvia photo and say: 'Last lesson we saw the grasshopper grow in steps because of its hard shell. Today we test whether every animal grows like that.' Pose the question, then give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds of silent thinking before sketching. Say: 'Draw what you honestly think; there are no wrong predictions today.' Circulate and note three or four different sketch types (straight line, staircase, curve). During pair talk say: 'Tell your partner why you chose that shape.' Cold-call 4 pairs with different sketches to draw theirs on the board, asking 'What reasoning led to that shape?' without evaluating. Keep all predictions visible to revisit.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share combined with the Predict step of Predict-Observe-Explain (POE). Committing to a prediction before seeing data exposes preconceptions (for example that all animals grow in a straight line or like insects). It creates cognitive conflict and a reason to examine the data later.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: each learner has a sketch with labelled axes and a one-sentence reason. Tally on the board how many predicted straight line, staircase, or S-curve. Look for the misconception 'growth is a constant straight-line increase' or 'all animals grow in steps'. No grades; use findings to adjust how much support is needed in the Observe phase.

framework.learnerExperience: (25 min) In groups of 4 with assigned roles (Data Recorder, Plotter, Calculator, Spokesperson - practising leadership and Unity), learners receive printed data sheets: Data Set A: Broiler chick mass (g) at weeks 0-10 from a Kiambu poultry farm; Data Set B: Child height (cm) from age 0-20 in Kenya; Data Set C: Grasshopper nymph body length (mm) over 60 days with moult days marked. Each group plots Set A on graph paper (mass against time), joins points with a smooth line, and labels where growth is slow, fastest, slowing and levelling. Using calculators and the formula Growth rate = (final value - initial value) / time interval, they calculate growth rate for four intervals: lag (e.g., weeks 0-1), exponential (e.g., weeks 3-6), deceleration (weeks 7-8) and stationary (weeks 9-10). They record answers with units (g/week) in a table. Faster groups plot Set B or C and compare. Learners note that the grasshopper graph stays flat between moults and jumps at moulting, unlike the smooth chick curve. If live grasshoppers are shown, they remain in ventilated containers and are handled gently.
framework.teacherMoves: Model the first calculation on the board: 'From week 3 at 300 g to week 4 at 520 g: (520 - 300) / 1 = 220 g per week.' Say: 'Always write the units.' Circulate with a checklist and ask oral probes: 'Which part of your graph is steepest? What does steepness tell you about the growth rate?' and 'Why is the growth rate near zero in the last weeks?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each probe. Check graph accuracy: axes labelled, uniform scale, points plotted correctly. Say: 'Check your partner's plot before you draw the line.' Ask each group: 'What happened at the moult days in Set C?' Remind groups with live insects to keep them shaded and release them correctly afterward. Provide print-based sheets for all groups and extra calculators for sharing. Support struggling groups with a partly completed table.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (Observe step) with data analysis: learners build the evidence themselves by plotting and calculating rather than being told the shape. Turning numbers into a graph and rates makes the four phases visible and quantifiable, and comparing Set A with Set C shows how a rigid exoskeleton changes the pattern.
framework.formativeAssessment: Growth curve graph check: use a quick checklist per group (axes labelled with units, even scales, points accurate within half a square, smooth S-shaped line, four phases labelled). Check the growth rate table: correct formula use and units (g/week). Oral probes: learners should say that exponential-phase growth rate is greatest and stationary-phase is near zero. Note groups who cannot connect steepness with rate for re-teaching.

framework.learnerExperience: (20 min) Gallery Walk: each group posts its graph and growth rate table on the wall. Groups rotate every 3 minutes with sticky notes giving one 'star' (what is correct) and one 'wish' (what could improve) using a peer rubric (accuracy of plot, correct calculation, clear phase labels). Back at their seats, each learner writes a CER response to the question: 'Why does the chick's graph form a smooth S-shape while the grasshopper's graph forms steps?' Claim: a one-sentence answer. Evidence: at least two data values or growth rates from the graphs. Reasoning: link to biology (the chick has no rigid exoskeleton so body cells and tissues can increase continuously; early growth is slow while the animal adjusts and has few cells, then cell division gives rapid growth, then resources and genetic limits slow growth until adult size is reached; the grasshopper's hard exoskeleton cannot stretch so size increases only after moulting). Learners then compare their weeks 0-10 graph with their earlier predictions and explain any change in thinking in pairs.
framework.teacherMoves: Before the walk say: 'Look for evidence, not just neatness.' Circulate during the Gallery Walk and listen for correct vocabulary. Model a CER on the board with another example: 'Claim: growth slows after week 8. Evidence: rate fell from 220 to 40 g/week. Reasoning: the chick is nearing its adult size set by genes and food intake.' Then say: 'Now write yours.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners to read their reasoning and ask 'Who can add to that?' Probe: 'Why is the lag phase slow if the chick is young and about to grow?' Address misconceptions directly: 'Does the insect melt and rebuild? What does our data say about the steps?' Link to the phenomenon: 'So the grasshopper's exuvia is the cost of having a hard, non-stretching shell.' Collect the CER responses for review.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) modelling together with Gallery Walks for peer review. Gallery Walks let learners see multiple representations and correct each other's errors, while CER forces them to justify the pattern with data and biological mechanism, linking the sigmoid curve to cell division, resource limits and the exoskeleton.
framework.formativeAssessment: Peer rubric (stars and wishes) completed for at least two other groups. CER responses: scoring indicators - claim addresses smooth versus stepped growth; evidence includes at least two numerical values with units; reasoning mentions cell division, limiting factors or adult size, and the exoskeleton. Cold-call responses show whether learners can name the four phases in order. Exit ticket (given in the final 5 minutes): 1) Name the phase with the highest growth rate. 2) Calculate the growth rate if a calf rose from 40 kg to 70 kg in 10 weeks. 3) Write one question about what makes an insect start to moult.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) Learners revisit the Driving Question Board with the central question: 'How does an animal outgrow its own hard shell, and why do some animals radically change shape while others just grow bigger?' Each learner writes one new question on a sticky note from today's work (for example: 'What tells the grasshopper nymph that it is time to moult?', 'Why do chicks stop growing at a certain size?', 'Do caterpillars show a sigmoid curve?', 'What controls the sudden jumps in the insect graph?'). They post it under the headings Growth Pattern, Control of Growth, and Metamorphosis. The class then moves earlier questions that today's evidence answered (for example, 'Do all animals grow the same way?') to an 'Answered' section, with the evidence cited.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take 2 minutes to write a question that today's graphs made you wonder.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before writing starts. Cold-call 4 learners to read and place questions, asking 'Which category does this fit, and why?' Move answered questions and ask 'What evidence from today lets us move it?' Highlight and read aloud the questions about what triggers and controls timing: 'Many of you ask what makes the insect moult at that moment. That is exactly our next investigation.' Keep the board visible in the classroom.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with Think-Pair-Share: pairs briefly share their questions before posting. Posting and categorising questions shows learners that evidence generates new questions and gives them ownership of the learning path into Lesson 4.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: every learner posts at least one question; at least some questions move from 'what' to 'what causes/controls' (higher-level thinking). Note the number of questions on hormonal control as a sign of readiness for Lesson 4. Listen to whether the reasoning given for moving answered questions cites data.

framework.learnerExperience: (15 min) In their groups, learners revise the class model of animal growth begun in Lessons 1-2. On a large sheet they add a new section: two side-by-side graphs (a smooth S-curve labelled with lag, exponential, deceleration, stationary phases and a staircase curve for the moulting insect) plus arrows and labels explaining why they differ (no rigid shell versus exoskeleton, cell division, limiting factors). They add the formula for growth rate with one worked example from their data. They use a different colour for new ideas and mark with a question mark the part they cannot yet explain: what triggers and controls the timing of moulting and metamorphosis. Groups quickly present for 1 minute to another group, who give feedback using the peer rubric.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use a different colour for what we learned today so we can see how our thinking is changing.' Circulate and ask: 'Where on your model does the exuvia appear? What does the flat part of the insect graph represent?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 3 groups to explain one change they made and why. Prompt for gaps: 'What in your model explains the timing of the steps? What is still missing?' Affirm that the question marks are scientific honesty. Close by saying: 'We now know how the growth patterns differ, but not what controls them. In Lesson 4 we investigate what triggers and controls the precise timing of moulting and metamorphosis in insects.' Remind learners that any live insects must be released gently where they were collected.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision with peer feedback (Gallery Walk style group presentations). Revising a visible model forces learners to integrate new quantitative evidence with earlier ideas, and marking unknowns turns gaps into the next investigation, supporting Creativity and Imagination as they adjust and rethink ideas.
framework.formativeAssessment: Peer rubrics during presentations: model includes both curve types, four phases labelled correctly, growth rate formula with worked example, explanation connecting shell/no shell to the pattern, and at least one unanswered question. Oral probes during group modelling: learners can explain why the insect graph is flat between moults. Collect the exit tickets; a correct calculation of 3 kg per week and identification of the exponential phase show mastery.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners could connect steepness of the graph to growth rate, and who still treated the curve as a picture? Did the predictions show the misconception that all animals grow like insects or in a straight line? Were the print-based data sets and calculators enough for every group to finish four growth rate calculations, and which interval was hardest? Did the comparison between the chick and the grasshopper clarify the effect of the exoskeleton? How many DQB questions asked about control or triggers, and is the class ready for hormones in Lesson 4? If live insects were used, were they handled kindly and released safely at the point of collection?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We plotted mass and height data for a Kenyan broiler chick, a child, and a grasshopper nymph. The chick and child graphs formed smooth S-shaped curves, while the grasshopper's length stayed flat and jumped at each moult.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Vertebrates and soft-bodied animals grow continuously in a sigmoid curve with lag, exponential, deceleration and stationary phases. Growth rate = (final value - initial value) / time interval, and it is highest in the exponential phase and near zero in the stationary phase. Hard-shelled insects show intermittent, stepwise growth because the exoskeleton cannot stretch.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The chick has no rigid shell, so cells can divide and increase size continuously: slow at first, then rapid, then slowing as it nears adult size set by genes and resources. The grasshopper must shed its exoskeleton (leaving the exuvia) before it can grow, so its size increases in steps. What triggers and controls the timing of moulting and metamorphosis is still unanswered and is the focus of Lesson 4.
