LESSONS.title: Hormones as the Control Switches of Moulting and Metamorphosis
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 3.2: Growth and Development in Animals
LESSONS.aresKeywords: ecdysone, juvenile hormone, brain hormone (PTTH), prothoracic gland, corpora allata, moulting, ecdysis, exuvia, larva, pupa, imago, metamorphosis, hormone concentration, gland removal, hormone injection

slo.purpose: To help learners figure out that the hormones Ecdysone, Juvenile Hormone and Brain Hormone interact to regulate moulting and stage transitions in insect life cycles, and so explain how a grasshopper or cicada can leave its hard exuvia behind and why some insects change shape completely while others only grow bigger.
slo.knowledge: Learners: (b) describe the role of hormones in growth and development in insects. They will explain that Brain Hormone from neurosecretory cells signals the prothoracic glands to release Ecdysone, which triggers moulting, and that Juvenile Hormone from the corpora allata decides what kind of moult occurs (larva to larva when JH is high, larva to pupa when JH is low, pupa to adult when JH is absent).
slo.skills: Searching for information on insect hormones from reference texts and digital devices; analysing experimental flowcharts showing gland removal and hormone injection in larvae; Developing and using models (SEP); Analysing and interpreting data (SEP); Constructing explanations using Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (SEP). Core competency: Digital Literacy, where learners appropriately select reliable sources on insect hormones. Print-based data sheets are provided where connectivity is limited.
slo.attitudes: Love: handle insects and specimens with compassion. Unity: collaborate with peers when analysing flowcharts. PCI Good governance: demonstrate principles of leadership (rotating roles of reader, recorder, reporter, timekeeper) while working with peers to search for information on insect hormones and their roles in growth and development. PCI Animal Welfare: treat animals with care.
slo.keyInquiry: How does growth in animals occur?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1-3 established that insects grow in steps (intermittent growth shown by growth curves and growth rates calculated in Lesson 3), and that some insects undergo complete metamorphosis while others undergo incomplete metamorphosis. Lesson 4 answers the 'what controls it?' question: hormones interact like a control system. This lesson gives the mechanism behind the exuvia beside the newly emerged grasshopper or cicada. It raises the new question for Lesson 5: Can visual animations help us see how hormone concentration balances dictate larva-to-pupa shifts?
slo.safetyNotes: Only observe live insects already collected for earlier lessons, or use preserved exuvia, from the school garden. Follow national animal welfare standards: collect only a few insects by hand or with a soft net, never kill, injure, freeze or pin insects for this lesson, keep them in ventilated containers with leaves of their food plant (maize or sukuma wiki), keep them in shade, wash hands before and after handling, and release them at the point of capture within 24 hours. Gland removal and hormone injection are studied ONLY through flowcharts and data sheets; no learner performs surgery or injections on any animal. Do not handle insects if a learner has an allergy; assign that learner to the reader or recorder role. Check that device use stays on approved educational sites.

LESSONS.overview: Learners return to the anchoring phenomenon: the empty split exuvia beside a larger newly emerged grasshopper or cicada, and a caterpillar that becomes a motionless pupa. They predict what inside the insect could 'tell' it when to moult and when to change shape. In groups they search reference texts, hormone function flowcharts and digital sources (or print data sheets) to identify Brain Hormone, Ecdysone and Juvenile Hormone, then analyse experimental flowcharts of gland removal and hormone injection in larvae (for example: removing the head/brain region, tying off the body, removing the corpora allata, injecting extra JH). They use Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) to explain how the hormones interact, add the mechanism to the class model and the Driving Question Board, and leave with a new question about how hormone concentration balances change over time, which leads to animations in Lesson 5.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at the exuvia and the newly emerged grasshopper or cicada (specimen or photo) and a photo of a maize-leaf armyworm or other caterpillar becoming a pupa. Individually they write for 2 minutes: 'What might be inside the insect's body that tells it WHEN to moult and WHETHER to change into a completely different shape?' They then use Think-Pair-Share, and in groups predict what would happen to a caterpillar if the part that sends the 'moult' signal were removed. Predictions are recorded on a POE sheet (Predict column) with a sketch.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the exuvia and say: 'Last lesson we saw that growth happens in steps. Today we ask: who or what is the boss that switches these steps on?' Pose the question and give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds in silence before anyone writes. Give 2 minutes of silent writing, then 2 minutes pair talk. Cold-call 4 pairs (not volunteers): 'Pair 3, what did your partner predict and why?' Probe with: 'What makes you think so?' and 'Where in your own body do signals that control growth, like at puberty, come from?' Record 4-5 predictions on the board without judging them. Note misconceptions such as 'the shell just peels like sunburned skin' or 'caterpillars melt with no control'. Ask: 'If the signal were removed, what do you predict happens to the caterpillar?' Wait 10-15 seconds again.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) and Think-Pair-Share. Predicting first makes prior ideas visible and creates a need to know; Think-Pair-Share gives every learner rehearsal time so the cold-calls are fair and the class sees a range of ideas to test against evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: every learner has a written prediction and a sketch on the POE sheet; at least 4 different predictions are shared; teacher tallies on the board how many predict a chemical or hormone-type signal versus 'the insect decides', temperature only, or 'the shell breaks by itself'. Look for learners linking to human puberty hormones as a sign of transfer from Form 1-3 ideas.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A (15 min): In groups of 4 with rotating leadership roles (reader, recorder, reporter, timekeeper), learners search reference texts, hormone function flowcharts and digital research devices (or print data sheets) to complete a 3-row table: Brain Hormone (PTTH), Ecdysone, Juvenile Hormone, with columns for where made, what it does, and when it is high or low. Part B (20 min): Groups analyse four experimental flowcharts on larvae (for example Experiment 1: larva with brain/neurosecretory cells removed, leading to no moult; Experiment 2: same larva injected with Ecdysone, leading to moult resumes; Experiment 3: young larva with extra Juvenile Hormone injected, leading to moults into a larger larva, not a pupa; Experiment 4: larva with corpora allata removed early, leading to a small, early pupa). They write what was changed, what happened, and what it shows. Relevant Kenyan context: the maize stalk borer or armyworm caterpillars on farms in the Rift Valley and the desert locust or grasshoppers (incomplete metamorphosis, nymphs) that moult several times. Learners then compare with the school-garden exuvia and discuss why the grasshopper nymph shows fewer shape changes (JH stays present until the final moult to adult).
framework.teacherMoves: Circulate with a checklist. Before starting say: 'Choose reliable sources: a textbook, a teacher-approved site, or the print sheet. Note the source name.' Remind about animal welfare: 'The live insects stay in their ventilated containers in the shade; we study the experiments on paper, not on living animals.' Give each group 2 minutes to read each flowchart silently, then WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before group discussion. Ask probes: 'What was the variable the scientist changed?' 'What was the control?' 'What does this result show about which gland sends the first signal?' Help a group that is stuck with: 'Follow the arrows: which gland acts first, which second?' Pause the class after Experiment 2 and cold-call 3 groups: 'What do you now say about the role of Ecdysone?' Support learners with limited connectivity by giving print sheets and pairing devices. After Experiment 4, cold-call 3 groups: 'Why does low JH change the type of moult?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (Observe) with data analysis of flowcharts. Comparing 'gland removed' with 'hormone replaced' is the logic of a controlled experiment, so learners can infer cause and effect rather than just memorize hormone names.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: the hormone table is complete with correct sources noted; learners correctly identify the variable changed and the result in at least 3 of the 4 flowcharts; oral probes during group work show learners say 'when X was removed, Y stopped, so X is needed for Y'; leadership roles rotate (check the group role sheet); teacher checks for the common error of swapping the functions of Ecdysone (triggers moulting) and JH (maintains the larval state).

framework.learnerExperience: Individually then in pairs, learners write a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) statement answering: 'How does the grasshopper or cicada outgrow its hard exuvia, and what decides whether an insect becomes another larva or a pupa?' Teacher models a CER on a different example first (for example, why a locust nymph stays a nymph through 4-5 moults). Pairs then draw a flow diagram linking: Brain Hormone, prothoracic gland, Ecdysone, moult, and Juvenile Hormone high or low, giving larva-to-larva, larva-to-pupa, pupa-to-adult. Groups do a short Gallery Walk: charts are posted, learners leave sticky-note feedback ('one strength, one question') using a peer rubric on claim accuracy, use of the experimental evidence, and reasoning that uses the term 'hormone'.
framework.teacherMoves: Model a CER aloud: 'My claim is... My evidence from Experiment 2 is... My reasoning is that...'. Then say: 'Now you write your own. You have 5 minutes.' After writing give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before pair sharing. Cold-call 4 learners to read a claim aloud, asking 'Who can add evidence from a flowchart?' Challenge: 'Does your explanation say why the old skin has to be shed in a hard-shelled insect?' (The cuticle does not stretch; Ecdysone triggers a new cuticle to form and the old one to split, and the insect swells with air or water before the new one hardens.) Direct the Gallery Walk: 6 minutes, rotate every 2 minutes, with each learner placing at least 2 sticky notes. Debrief by cold-calling 3 groups: 'What was the strongest feedback you received?' Correct the misconception that insects 'melt and rebuild without control': say 'There is a hormone control system, and the signals decide each step.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) modelling and Gallery Walks. CER forces learners to link each claim to specific experimental evidence and a scientific reason, and the Gallery Walk uses peer review to expose gaps, so learners refine explanations before they commit to the class model.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators using the peer rubric (0-2 for each of claim, evidence, reasoning): a strong response states that Brain Hormone stimulates the prothoracic gland to release Ecdysone which triggers moulting, and that high JH keeps the larval form while low or absent JH allows pupation and adult emergence; cites at least one experimental result; and uses terms correctly. Teacher notes which groups reverse the roles of JH and Ecdysone for reteaching. Oral probes while groups present: 'What would happen if JH stayed high at the last larval moult?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board with the question 'How does an animal outgrow its own hard shell, and why do some animals radically change shape while others just grow bigger?'. In groups they write on sticky notes (1) one question now answered by today's evidence (move to the 'Answered' area with a note of the evidence), and (2) one new question. The expected new question is about how the changing amounts of the hormones over time cause the shift from larva to pupa, which leads to Lesson 5. Learners also sort earlier questions into 'answered', 'partly answered' and 'still to investigate'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at our board. Which questions can we now answer using today's flowcharts?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners to move a question and justify it with evidence from a specific experiment. Prompt for new questions: 'What do you still not understand about HOW MUCH of each hormone is present and WHEN?' Guide to the storyline question: 'Can visual animations help us see how hormone concentration balances dictate larva-to-pupa shifts?' Add it to the board in a different colour. Ask at least 2 learners with quieter voices (cold-call) to read out new questions.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board tracking. Moving questions between zones shows learners their own growing understanding and keeps the investigation learner-driven, while new questions create a purpose for Lesson 5.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: at least 3 earlier questions are correctly moved with a stated piece of evidence; each group contributes one new question that is testable or researchable; a question about hormone concentration or timing appears; exit ticket at the end (one sentence: 'Brain Hormone, Ecdysone and Juvenile Hormone work together by... ') is collected and sorted as secure, partial, or misconception.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the class and individual models of insect growth by adding the hormone control layer to their earlier model of intermittent growth (the stepped growth curve from Lesson 3) and life cycles. Using the grasshopper (incomplete metamorphosis: egg, nymph, adult) and a moth or butterfly such as the maize armyworm (complete: egg, larva, pupa, adult), they draw arrows showing where Brain Hormone, Ecdysone and JH act at each moult, and annotate the stepped growth curve to show that each upward step coincides with moulting (Ecdysone peaks) and the plateau with the hardened cuticle. They write a short caption: 'The exuvia is left behind because...'. Creativity and Imagination: learners adjust and rethink their ideas as they revise.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take out your model from Lesson 3. What is missing that explains who controls the steps?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then 8 minutes for revising. Circulate and ask during oral probes: 'Where on your growth curve does Ecdysone rise?' 'Why does the grasshopper nymph look like a small adult but the caterpillar does not?' Remind learners to mark what they changed in a different colour so revisions are visible. Cold-call 3 learners to share one change and the evidence that led them to it. Close by handing out the exit ticket, and point out the unanswered question: 'We now know WHICH hormones, but not HOW their amounts change over time. Next lesson we will watch animations to find out.' Remind learners to return all insects to the garden at the point of capture and wash hands.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision with a peer check. Adding the mechanism to a model learners already own shows that explanations are built and refined from evidence, and marking revisions in colour makes the change in thinking explicit.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: the revised model shows the correct order Brain Hormone, then prothoracic gland, then Ecdysone, then moult; shows JH high for larva-to-larva moults and low or absent for pupation and adult emergence; links moults to steps on the growth curve (growth curve graph check); distinguishes complete from incomplete metamorphosis using hormone action; colour-coded revisions are visible. Peer rubric during short presentations to a neighbouring group: accurate, evidence-linked, clear. Exit ticket collected and sorted.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson ask yourself: Did learners use the experimental flowcharts as evidence rather than reciting hormone names? Which groups swapped the roles of Ecdysone and Juvenile Hormone, and what reteaching is needed at the start of Lesson 5? Were cold-calls spread fairly, including learners without devices who used print sheets? Did the waiting time of 10-15 seconds produce deeper answers? Were all insects handled gently and returned to the garden, in line with national animal welfare standards? Did the math of growth rate from Lesson 3 appear correctly on the growth curve annotations? Which misconceptions (shell 'peels like sunburned skin', caterpillars 'melt' without control) persist, and what evidence will address them in the animations next lesson?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We analysed flowcharts of experiments on larvae: with the brain/neurosecretory cells removed the larva did not moult; with Ecdysone injected it moulted again; with extra Juvenile Hormone it moulted into another larva instead of a pupa; with the corpora allata removed early it formed a small pupa early. We also compared these with the empty exuvia and the larger grasshopper or cicada from the school garden.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Brain Hormone signals the prothoracic glands to release Ecdysone, which triggers moulting. Juvenile Hormone decides the kind of moult: high levels keep the larval form, low levels allow pupation, and none allows adult emergence. Hormones interact like a control system, so moulting and shape change are regulated and not random.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The grasshopper or cicada outgrows its hard shell because hormones trigger a new, larger cuticle to form beneath the old one, the old one splits and is left as the exuvia, and the insect expands before the new cuticle hardens, so growth happens in steps. Insects with complete metamorphosis, like caterpillars, change shape completely because Juvenile Hormone falls and allows pupation, while grasshopper nymphs keep JH until the last moult and so look like small adults.

LESSONS.title: The Chemical Switch: How Juvenile Hormone Decides Whether an Insect Stays Young or Becomes an Adult
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 3.2: Growth and Development in Animals
LESSONS.aresKeywords: juvenile hormone, ecdysone, moulting, ecdysis, metamorphosis, nymph, larva, pupa, imago, exuvia, endocrine gland, corpora allata, prothoracic gland, feedback, flow diagram

slo.purpose: To help learners use digital animations to explain how fluctuating Juvenile Hormone (JH) levels, working with the moulting hormone ecdysone, decide whether an insect moults into another nymph/larva or transitions into a pupa/adult, and so explain the empty exuvia and the grasshopper-versus-butterfly puzzle from the school garden.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (b) describe the role of hormones in growth and development in insects; state that ecdysone triggers moulting while the level of JH determines the type of moult (high JH = nymph/larva to nymph/larva; falling JH = pupa then adult); contrast hormonal control in incomplete metamorphosis (grasshopper) and complete metamorphosis (butterfly/moth).
slo.skills: Digital Literacy: the learner appropriately selects animations illustrating the effect of hormones on insect growth and development. Creativity and Imagination: the learner adjusts and rethinks their ideas while building flow diagrams. NGSS SEP: Developing and Using Models; Obtaining, Evaluating and Communicating Information; Constructing Explanations (CER).
slo.attitudes: Love: the learner handles insects and living specimens with compassion. Unity: the learner collaborates with others while building and reviewing flow diagrams. Good governance (PCI): the learner demonstrates leadership principles by taking rotating roles (selector, recorder, presenter, timekeeper) while searching for information on insect hormones. Animal Welfare (PCI): the learner treats animals with care.
slo.keyInquiry: How does growth in animals occur?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1-4 established that insects grow in stages, that the exoskeleton restricts growth so growth is intermittent (step-like) in the growth curve, and that moulting occurs. Growth rates were calculated in Lesson 3 using the standard formula: growth rate = change in measurement ÷ change in time. This lesson supplies the CAUSE: a chemical control system. It explains why the same moulting process produces a bigger nymph in a grasshopper but a pupa in a butterfly. It raises the next question: How do all these growth patterns and chemical controls ensure animal survival and species continuity?
slo.safetyNotes: Animal welfare: if live insects are shown (e.g., grasshoppers or caterpillars collected from the school garden or maize field), collect only a few by hand or soft container, handle gently, keep in ventilated containers with fresh leaves (sukuma wiki or maize leaves), never pin, crush or leave in the sun, and return them to the exact place of collection within the lesson/day. Wash hands after handling. Do not collect protected species, and do not handle stinging or hairy caterpillars with bare hands (use a leaf or paper to move them). Projector cables and devices should be kept away from walkways. Where internet is limited, use pre-downloaded animations or print-based sheets.

LESSONS.overview: Learners return to the empty exuvia beside the larger newly emerged grasshopper and the motionless pupa of a butterfly. They predict what 'switch' inside the insect decides whether it stays a nymph/larva or becomes an adult. They then select and view digital animations (pre-downloaded on the teacher's device or projected; print-based storyboard sheets as the offline alternative) showing hormonal regulation of insect metamorphosis, record evidence, and synthesise it in flow diagrams on templates. A gallery walk with peer rubrics and CER statements consolidates understanding. The DQB is updated and the class model of 'how an insect outgrows its shell' is revised to include hormones. The lesson ends with an exit ticket and the question for Lesson 6 on survival and species continuity.

framework.learnerExperience: (approx. 12 min) Learners look at the phenomenon display: an exuvia from the school garden on a maize leaf, a photo of the newly emerged larger grasshopper, and photos of a caterpillar, a pupa and a butterfly (e.g., a African monarch/ common citrus swallowtail from Kakamega or Kisumu gardens). Individually they write in their notebooks a prediction: 'What inside the insect's body tells it to moult, and what decides whether the next stage is a bigger nymph/larva or a pupa/adult?' They sketch a quick 'prediction model' with arrows. They do Think-Pair-Share, then share with the class.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the exuvia/photos. Say: 'Remember the empty skin on the maize leaf. Grasshopper nymphs come out looking like small adults, but the caterpillar becomes a pupa. Something is controlling this. Write your prediction silently for 2 minutes.' Then: 'Turn to your partner and share for 1 minute each.' Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking: 'What could be the signal inside the body that tells the insect which type of moult to make?' Cold-call 4 pairs (not volunteers) including at least 2 who have not spoken in earlier lessons. Say: 'Thank you, I am not judging right or wrong; we will test these ideas with evidence.' Record 3-4 prediction ideas on the board (e.g., 'temperature', 'food', 'a chemical in the blood', 'age'). Address the misconception that caterpillars 'melt and rebuild without control' by asking: 'If it is without control, why does it always make a butterfly and not something else?' (WAIT 10 seconds).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) and Think-Pair-Share: committing to a prediction first creates a cognitive 'need to know' and makes learners notice where the animations confirm or challenge their thinking. Pairing lets learners rehearse and refine ideas safely before public sharing.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) at least 80% of learners have a written prediction with a drawn arrow model before pair-sharing; (2) teacher listens in on 5 pairs and tallies who mentions 'hormone/chemical', 'brain', 'gland', 'food' or 'temperature'; (3) misconceptions noted ('insects peel like sunburnt skin', 'melt and rebuild') on a quick checklist to revisit at the exit ticket.

framework.learnerExperience: (approx. 25 min) In groups of 4 with rotating roles (selector, recorder, presenter, timekeeper), learners select and view at least two digital animations from the teacher's list (e.g., 'Insect moulting and ecdysone', 'Hormonal control of metamorphosis in butterfly', 'Incomplete metamorphosis in locust/grasshopper'). The selector justifies why an animation is suitable using a 3-point checklist: scientifically accurate, shows hormone levels, shows both complete and incomplete metamorphosis. The recorder fills an observation table with columns: Stage; Hormone(s) present; Level of JH (high/falling/low/absent); Result of moult. Groups without connectivity use the print storyboard sheets with JH-level graphs showing a JH curve across instars of a grasshopper and a butterfly across larva-pupa-adult. Learners also plot or read the JH-level curve against the stepwise growth curve from Lesson 3 and note that ecdysone peaks coincide with each step upward in size. Live specimens (grasshopper nymph, caterpillar) or preserved exuviae are available at one station for comparison and gentle observation only.
framework.teacherMoves: Before viewing, say: 'You are evidence hunters. Your job is not to watch passively but to capture what hormone is released, from where, and what happens to JH level at each moult.' Show the animations on the projector once through for the whole class, pausing at 3 key points to ask: 'What just happened to the JH level?' Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners per pause. Circulate and ask oral probes: 'Which gland released ecdysone? What would happen if JH stayed high at the last larval moult?' 'Where does your table show a difference between grasshopper and butterfly?' Remind learners: 'Handle the live insects with a soft leaf, gently, and they go back to the maize plants at the end.' Support groups using print sheets by checking they read the graph axes correctly. Assign leadership rotation: 'Every 8 minutes swap roles so every member practises leading.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (Observe): learners collect structured evidence to test their predictions. The structured observation table directs attention to the variable that matters (JH level) and builds the pattern 'high JH = stay juvenile; low JH = become adult'. Linking JH curves to the step-like growth curve integrates earlier lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Oral probes during group work: learner can correctly state at least one of 'ecdysone triggers moulting' and 'high JH keeps the juvenile form'. Growth curve graph check: teacher checks that groups correctly mark moulting points on the step-like curve and do not draw a smooth line. Observable indicators: tables completed with JH levels for all stages; groups justify animation choice using the checklist; roles rotated.

framework.learnerExperience: (approx. 25 min) Groups synthesise their findings into an interactive flow diagram using the flow chart template (digitally on devices, or with arrow cards and paper strips that can be moved around). The diagram must include: brain signals; prothoracic gland releasing ecdysone; corpora allata releasing JH; and two pathways (A) high JH: nymph/larva to larger nymph/larva; (B) JH falls: larva to pupa to adult (complete metamorphosis), or last nymph to adult (incomplete). Learners then write a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning statement answering: 'How does the same moulting process lead to a bigger grasshopper nymph in one case and a pupa in another?' Example claim: 'The level of JH decides the type of moult.' They then use the diagram to explain the exuvia in the school garden and why the new grasshopper is larger than the discarded skin (body expands before the new cuticle hardens). Then they hold a Gallery Walk: groups post diagrams, rotate every 3 minutes, and leave peer feedback sticky notes using the peer rubric (accuracy, completeness, clarity, creativity).
framework.teacherMoves: Model one CER example on the board using a different phenomenon: 'Claim: A locust nymph in a swarm in Turkana moults into another nymph. Evidence: JH level is high. Reasoning: High JH maintains juvenile features, so ecdysone-triggered moulting produces another nymph.' Say: 'Now write yours for the butterfly pupa.' Give 5 minutes. Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before cold-calling 3 groups to read claims. Probe: 'What is your evidence? Which part of the animation shows it?' 'What would you expect if JH were artificially added to a final-instar caterpillar?' (Expect: extra larval stage or a giant larva.) Link to Kenyan context: 'Scientists at icipe in Nairobi study insect hormones to control pests like locusts and the fall armyworm on maize farms.' Run the gallery walk: 'Read, then write one star (what is accurate) and one wish (what can be improved) on a sticky note. Be kind and specific.' Promote Unity: 'Give feedback that helps your classmates improve.' After the walk, ask 4 learners cold-call to report one idea they changed because of another group's diagram. Correct any misconceptions: JH is not the hormone that causes moulting; ecdysone is, and JH decides the kind of moult.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) modelling: separates what the learner believes from the data and the scientific principle, so explanations are accountable to evidence. Gallery Walk: peer review exposes learners to alternative representations and makes them revise and defend their reasoning (Creativity and Imagination: adjusting and rethinking ideas). Flow diagram: shows cause-and-effect and sequence of the hormonal control.
framework.formativeAssessment: Peer rubrics (4 criteria scored 1-3) during the gallery walk; teacher checks CER statements for: a claim naming JH level, evidence cited from an animation or graph, reasoning that links JH to type of moult. Observable indicators: diagram includes both pathways and correct labels of ecdysone and JH; learners can explain, without notes, why grasshoppers have no pupa stage; sticky notes give at least one specific comment. Success criterion: 75% of groups include ecdysone as the moult trigger and JH as the decider.

framework.learnerExperience: (approx. 8 min) Learners revisit the class Driving Question Board. In pairs, they review existing question cards and mark those now answered (e.g., 'Why does the caterpillar stop eating and become still?', 'What controls moulting?'). They write 1-2 new questions on cards, such as 'How do these growth patterns and chemical controls help the species survive?', 'Can farmers use JH chemicals to control pests such as armyworm on maize?', 'Do vertebrates like humans also use hormones for growth?' They place the cards on the board under categories: Answered, Partly answered, New.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at our board. Which questions can we now answer using the evidence from today? Come and move a card and explain why.' Cold-call 3 learners to move cards and justify using evidence. Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds when asking: 'What new question has today's evidence made you curious about?' Use cold-call for 3 learners to read their new questions. Highlight the question for Lesson 6 and read it aloud: 'How do all these growth patterns and chemical controls ensure animal survival and species continuity?' Praise questions linked to Kenyan contexts (pest control, locust swarms, silk moth rearing).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: DQB with Think-Pair-Share: learners see their own learning progress and generate authentic questions that drive the next investigation, which keeps the storyline coherent and student-owned.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: at least 5 cards moved with an evidence-based justification; at least 6 new, testable questions posted; teacher notes questions that reveal lingering misconceptions (e.g., 'melting without control').

framework.learnerExperience: (approx. 10 min) Learners revise their class/individual model of 'How does an insect outgrow its hard shell and why do some change shape completely?' Using the earlier model (exoskeleton, moulting, stepwise growth) they add: brain, prothoracic gland, corpora allata, ecdysone, JH, and the high-JH/low-JH pathways. They label their model for both a grasshopper and a butterfly, and annotate with a short note on what changed from their prediction. Individually they complete an exit ticket: (1) Which hormone triggers moulting? (2) What does a falling JH level cause in a butterfly caterpillar? (3) Draw or write why the grasshopper has no pupa stage. (4) One question you still have.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your model from Lesson 4. In a different colour, add what you learned about hormones today. Show the arrows and the JH levels.' Walk around with oral probes: 'Show me where JH is high in your model.' 'Why does the exuvia get left behind?' Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, and cold-call 3 learners to explain one revision to the class. Collect exit tickets at the door. Remind learners to return live insects to the garden gently and wash their hands. Give a bridging statement: 'Next time we ask why this whole system matters for survival and the continuation of the species.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision: learners integrate new evidence into a single explanatory model, make their thinking visible, and reflect on how their ideas have changed since the Predict Phase. Exit ticket provides individual accountability.
framework.formativeAssessment: Exit tickets: success if the learner names ecdysone as moulting trigger, JH as the determinant of the type of moult, and explains the absence of a pupa in incomplete metamorphosis. Observable indicators: model includes at least 4 new labelled components and a correct pathway for both insect types; learners can explain one change from their original prediction. Teacher sorts exit tickets into three piles (secure, partial, misconception) to plan re-teaching at the start of Lesson 6.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson consider: Did learners select animations using the checklist rather than choosing the most entertaining one? Which groups confused ecdysone with JH, and what evidence in the animation helped correct this? Did the print-based sheets give equal access to the evidence for learners without devices? Were live insects handled with care and returned safely, in line with national animal welfare standards? How well did learners connect hormone levels to the stepwise growth curves and the growth-rate calculations from Lesson 3 (rate = change in measurement ÷ change in time)? Did all learners participate in leadership roles? Which exit ticket misconceptions need to be revisited before Lesson 6?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We viewed animations and graphs showing ecdysone peaks before every moult, and JH levels that stay high during nymph/larval moults but fall before the pupa and adult stages. We also saw that grasshoppers go from nymph to adult without a pupa, while butterflies have a pupal stage. The exuvia in the garden is the old exoskeleton left after a moult.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Moulting is triggered by ecdysone, and the level of Juvenile Hormone decides what type of moult occurs: high JH means the insect moults into another nymph/larva, while falling JH leads to a pupa (complete metamorphosis) or an adult (incomplete metamorphosis). Growth is stepwise because the exoskeleton must be shed before the insect can get bigger. Metamorphosis is a controlled, hormone-regulated process, not 'melting without control'.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: An insect outgrows its hard shell by releasing ecdysone, which causes it to shed its old exoskeleton and expand before the new one hardens. A grasshopper keeps a high-to-declining JH level through several nymph moults and becomes an adult without a pupa, while a butterfly caterpillar's JH falls dramatically before it forms a pupa and then an adult, which is why some animals change shape completely and others just grow bigger.

LESSONS.title: Final Explanation: Controlled Growth, Metamorphosis and Survival in Kenyan Insects
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 3.2: Growth and Development in Animals
LESSONS.aresKeywords: exuvia, moulting, ecdysis, ecdysone, juvenile hormone, complete metamorphosis, incomplete metamorphosis, nymph, pupa, growth curve, intermittent growth, sigmoid growth, Claim-Evidence-Reasoning

slo.purpose: To consolidate evidence from Lessons 1-5 into a final scientific explanation of how an insect outgrows its hard exoskeleton and why some insects change shape completely while others only grow bigger, and to compare the final model with the Day 1 model.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: a) distinguish between complete and incomplete metamorphosis in insects; b) describe the role of hormones (ecdysone and juvenile hormone) in growth and development in insects; c) analyse growth curves in animals (continuous and intermittent growth); d) appreciate the importance of growth and development in animals.
slo.skills: Constructing evidence-based explanations (CER); revising and comparing models; interpreting intermittent (step-like) and sigmoid growth curves and using the standard growth rate formula (change in measurement divided by time, as taught in Lesson 3); communicating scientific ideas through posters and gallery walks; giving and receiving peer feedback using a rubric.
slo.attitudes: Love: handles insects and specimens with compassion. Unity: collaborates with peers when building CER posters and giving peer review. Good governance (PCI): demonstrates leadership in group roles (facilitator, recorder, presenter, materials manager). Animal Welfare (PCI): treats animals with care. Core competencies: Creativity and Imagination (adjusts and rethinks ideas while revising models); Digital Literacy (selects appropriate animations or print data sheets when internet is limited).
slo.keyInquiry: How does growth in animals occur?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the final lesson of the unit. Learners return to the anchoring phenomenon (an empty grasshopper or cicada exuvia with a split down the back beside a larger newly emerged insect, and caterpillars becoming pupae then butterflies) and use all evidence to answer the Driving Question. Their Final Explanation shows that controlled growth and developmental transitions allow animals to optimize resource use, reduce parent-offspring competition, and survive harsh environments. It closes with a new question for extension: How might human pesticides disrupt these exact hormonal pathways in agricultural pests?
slo.safetyNotes: Handle all specimens and exuviae gently; wash hands with soap and water after handling. Any live insects collected from the school garden (maize leaves, sukuma wiki plants, tree bark) must be collected without harm following national animal welfare standards: collect only the minimum needed, use ventilated containers with leaves and a little moisture, avoid crowding, never expose to direct sun or heat, do not pin, crush or kill for display, and return all live insects to the exact place of collection at the end of the lesson. Empty exuviae may be used freely. Learners with allergies to insect bites or pollen should wear gloves or observe from photos. Keep walkways clear during the gallery walk.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin by predicting how their Day 1 model would change after what they have learned, then observe their original Day 1 models side by side with evidence from Lessons 1-5 (exuvia samples, life-cycle models, hormone animations or print summaries, and growth curve graphs of grasshopper/nymph length against time showing step-like growth). They construct Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) posters answering the Driving Question, take part in a Gallery Walk with peer rubrics, complete the Driving Question Board (DQB) by sorting sticky notes into answered and new questions, and revise their models into a final model with a Day 1 versus final comparison. An exit ticket checks individual understanding and the lesson ends with the new question about pesticides and insect hormones.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at the anchoring phenomenon displayed on the board: a photo or real exuvia from a maize leaf beside a larger newly emerged grasshopper or cicada, plus a photo of a caterpillar, pupa and butterfly. Individually, in 3 minutes, they write a prediction on a sticky note: 'If I redrew my Day 1 model today, the three biggest things I would change are...' Then they Think-Pair-Share with a partner and predict which parts of the Driving Question they can now answer fully, partly or not yet.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the phenomenon and say: 'Remember the empty skin we found on the maize leaf? Look carefully at the skin and the insect next to it. Today you will explain how this insect outgrew its own hard shell, and why a butterfly looks nothing like its caterpillar while a grasshopper nymph looks like a small adult.' Give 3 minutes of silent writing. Then say: 'Turn to your partner and share your predictions for 2 minutes.' Circulate and listen. Cold-call 4 pairs: 'What would you change in your Day 1 model?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds after each question before calling on anyone. Record common predictions on the board under 'What we think we know now'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share combined with Predict-Observe-Explain (POE): predicting before revisiting evidence makes learners activate their ideas from Lessons 1-5 and exposes remaining misconceptions (for example, that insects peel like sunburned skin or that caterpillars melt and rebuild without control), so that the next phase of observation has a purpose.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: the sticky note names at least two specific changes (for example, adding hormones, showing the old exoskeleton splitting, or adding a pupal stage); learners use vocabulary such as moulting, ecdysone or nymph; during pairing, both partners speak. Teacher records on a tally sheet which learners still mention peeling or melting, to target in later phases.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of four with assigned roles (facilitator, recorder, materials manager, presenter), learners revisit their evidence folders: (1) their original Day 1 models; (2) exuviae or photos of grasshopper and cicada moults; (3) their life-cycle models of complete metamorphosis (for example butterfly, housefly or mosquito from Lake Victoria region) and incomplete metamorphosis (grasshopper, cockroach); (4) the hormone summary (ecdysone triggers moulting, juvenile hormone keeps the juvenile form) from animations or print-based data sheets; (5) growth curve graphs from Lesson 3 showing intermittent (step-like) growth in insect body length and sigmoid growth in other animals such as a calf or a chicken. Each group lists on a table the evidence that explains: why the insect growth curve has steps, what happens at each moult, and how complete and incomplete metamorphosis differ. They recalculate one growth rate from the graph using the standard formula from Lesson 3 (growth rate = change in length ÷ time taken) for a step phase and a flat phase.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your evidence folders. Your job is to be detectives: find three pieces of evidence that explain the empty skin.' Distribute print-based data sheets to groups without connectivity or tablets. Walk around and probe orally: 'Where on your graph does the moult happen? Why is the line flat between the steps?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds before prompting further. Ask: 'What does juvenile hormone do in a caterpillar compared with ecdysone?' Cold-call 3 groups to state one piece of evidence each. Remind learners of animal welfare: any live insects are handled gently in ventilated containers and will be returned to the garden at the end of the lesson. Check that the growth rate calculation uses the formula from Lesson 3 with correct units (mm per day).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (observe step): learners compare their earlier predictions and Day 1 models with actual data from the exuviae, life-cycle models and graphs. Linking a flat section of the graph to a rigid exoskeleton and a vertical step to the moment of moulting helps learners see growth as controlled and intermittent, not smooth.
framework.formativeAssessment: Growth curve graph check: teacher checks that each group has correctly labelled axes with units, identified a step (moult) and a plateau (hard exoskeleton), and calculated one growth rate accurately using the standard formula. Oral probe indicators: learners correctly state that ecdysone triggers moulting and that high juvenile hormone gives another nymph or larval stage while low levels allow pupation or adult formation. Record groups that confuse complete and incomplete metamorphosis for reteaching.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group builds a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) poster on chart paper answering the Driving Question: 'How does an animal outgrow its own hard shell, and why do some animals radically change shape while others just grow bigger?' Claim: a one- or two-sentence answer. Evidence: at least three pieces drawn from the exuviae, life-cycle models, hormone information and growth curve data (including the calculated growth rates). Reasoning: a scientific explanation linking the evidence to the claim, including why controlled growth and developmental transitions help insects optimize resource use (for example, a caterpillar feeding on sukuma wiki leaves while the adult butterfly drinks nectar), reduce parent-offspring competition for food, and survive harsh environments (for example, a pupa or egg surviving the dry season in the Rift Valley). Groups then take part in a Gallery Walk: posters stay up, two members rotate to read other posters and give feedback using a peer rubric while two stay to explain.
framework.teacherMoves: Model one short CER example on the board using a different Kenyan context first (for example, why locusts moult several times): 'My claim is..., my evidence is..., my reasoning connects the evidence to the claim because...'. Give 20 minutes for poster construction. Say: 'Your reasoning must answer why, not just what.' Circulate and ask: 'How does your evidence support your claim?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds. Then start the Gallery Walk: 'Rotate clockwise every 3 minutes. Leave one star (a strength) and one question on a sticky note for each poster.' Cold-call 5 learners afterwards: 'What was the strongest piece of evidence you saw on another poster?' Give groups 4 minutes to read the feedback and revise their posters.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) modelling and Gallery Walk peer review: CER forces learners to connect data to scientific ideas rather than just stating facts, and the Gallery Walk exposes them to alternative explanations, so that they strengthen their reasoning and correct remaining misconceptions through discussion with peers.
framework.formativeAssessment: Peer rubric (4 criteria scored 1-3): claim answers both parts of the Driving Question; at least three accurate pieces of evidence; reasoning links hormones to moulting and to metamorphosis type; explanation of survival advantage (resource use, reduced competition, harsh environments). Observable indicators: posters state that the old exoskeleton is replaced, not peeled like skin; hormones are named; a stage-by-stage contrast between complete (egg, larva, pupa, adult) and incomplete (egg, nymph, adult) metamorphosis appears. Teacher uses the rubric to spot-check the weakest two posters and offers a prompt for revision.

framework.learnerExperience: The class returns to the Driving Question Board that has been built since Lesson 1. Learners move their sticky-note questions into three columns: 'Answered (with evidence)', 'Partly answered', and 'New questions'. For each answered question, one volunteer attaches a short evidence note (a line from the CER poster). Learners add new questions that arise, for example: 'How might human pesticides disrupt these exact hormonal pathways in agricultural pests?' and 'Do other animals, such as crabs in Mombasa, moult like insects?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Let's look at our board together. Which questions can we now answer, and what is our evidence?' Allow learners to move their own notes. Cold-call 6 learners to justify why they placed a question in a column: 'What evidence tells you this question is answered?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds before accepting responses. Highlight the new question on pesticides and hormones: 'This is where science goes next. Farmers in Kericho, Kisumu and the Rift Valley use pesticides on crops. What might happen if a chemical mimics juvenile hormone or blocks ecdysone?' Record the new question prominently as the bridge to future learning.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: DQB completion with evidence-linking: tying each question to evidence shows learners how their understanding has grown across the unit and reinforces that science is an ongoing process in which answers lead to new questions.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: learners correctly sort at least 80% of questions and justify placements with specific evidence; new questions use unit vocabulary and are testable (for example, involve hormones, life stages or pesticides). Teacher checks the number of learners who contributed to the board and notes which questions remain 'partly answered' to address in revision.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner takes out their Day 1 model of how the insect outgrew its shell and creates a revised Final Model on a fresh sheet or on the reverse side, using labelled drawings and arrows. The final model must show: the exoskeleton and why it cannot stretch; hormonal signals (ecdysone and juvenile hormone) triggering moulting; the new, soft, larger exoskeleton hardening after the moult; the intermittent growth curve; and a comparison of complete versus incomplete metamorphosis with a Kenyan example of each. Learners then complete a 'Day 1 vs Final' comparison table with three columns: What I thought on Day 1, What I know now, and What evidence changed my thinking. Finally they complete an exit ticket.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take your Day 1 model. With a different coloured pen, show every change that your evidence supports.' Allow 15 minutes of individual work, then 5 minutes of Think-Pair-Share to compare changes. Circulate with oral probes: 'Where does the hormone act in your model?' 'Why does a caterpillar not simply grow like a calf?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 learners to explain one change. Distribute the exit ticket: '1) In two sentences explain how an insect outgrows its exoskeleton. 2) Name one advantage of complete metamorphosis. 3) One question I still have.' Remind learners that live insects must be returned to the garden gently. Close by reading aloud the next question: 'How might human pesticides disrupt these exact hormonal pathways in agricultural pests?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision with Day 1 versus Final comparison: making learners visibly change a model, rather than starting anew, shows how evidence changes ideas and builds metacognition about their own learning. Think-Pair-Share supports peer clarification of the final model.
framework.formativeAssessment: Exit ticket and model check. Success indicators: the final model shows a moulting step with hormone labels; explains that growth happens in bursts after moulting rather than smoothly; distinguishes complete from incomplete metamorphosis correctly; includes at least one survival advantage (less competition for food between larva and adult, dormancy in a pupa during dry or cold conditions, efficient use of resources). Day 1 versus Final table includes at least three specific, evidence-based changes. Learners who fail to name hormones or still say that insects 'peel' or 'melt' receive follow-up support.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which groups could move from describing what happens (moulting, metamorphosis) to explaining why it happens using hormones and survival advantages? Which misconceptions (insects peeling like sunburned skin, caterpillars melting and rebuilding without control) persisted in posters or models, and what evidence would address them? Did the growth rate calculations follow the standard formula from Lesson 3 consistently, and could learners interpret the steps and plateaus on the growth curve? Were the animal welfare guidelines for local insect collection followed and all live specimens returned? How effectively did the print-based data sheets support groups without internet access? What follow-up activity could connect the pesticide question to local farming practices in Kenya?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed an empty exuvia with a split down its back beside a larger newly emerged grasshopper or cicada, caterpillars becoming pupae and butterflies, and insect growth curves with steps and flat sections. We also observed how our Day 1 models differed from our final models.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that an insect's hard exoskeleton cannot stretch, so the insect moults (ecdysis) under hormone control: ecdysone triggers moulting and juvenile hormone determines whether the next stage stays juvenile or develops toward the adult. This produces intermittent growth. Incomplete metamorphosis (egg, nymph, adult) gives small adult-like nymphs, while complete metamorphosis (egg, larva, pupa, adult) gives very different life stages that use different foods and survive harsh conditions.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can explain that an animal outgrows its hard shell by making a new, larger exoskeleton beneath the old one, then splitting and leaving the old exuvia while the new one is still soft and expandable. Controlled hormone-regulated growth and developmental transitions help animals optimize resource use, reduce competition between young and adults, and survive harsh environments. New question: How might human pesticides disrupt these exact hormonal pathways in agricultural pests?

FINAL_EXPLANATION.subjectLabel: Biology Grade 11: Growth and Development in Animals (3.2)
FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions: Use this document as a model for your own Final Explanation. Your task is to answer the driving question: How does an animal outgrow its own hard shell, and why do some animals radically change shape while others just grow bigger? Build a CER (Claim, Evidence, Reasoning) poster with an annotated graphical model. Anchor every section in the phenomenon: the empty, split exuvia beside a larger, newly emerged grasshopper or cicada on a maize leaf or tree bark in your school garden, and the caterpillar that becomes a pupa and then a butterfly. Use evidence from your six lessons, such as growth curves, observations of exuviae, and hormone diagrams. Write in your own words and label all graphs and diagrams clearly.

sections.title: 1. Claim: Answering the Driving Question
sections.prompt: State in 2-3 sentences how an animal outgrows a hard shell and why some animals change shape completely while others only grow bigger. Mention the two growth patterns and the role of hormones.
sections.exemplar: An insect outgrows its hard shell by shedding it in a process called ecdysis (moulting). The shell cannot stretch, so the insect grows in sudden steps each time it sheds the old shell and swells before the new one hardens. Animals with a hard exoskeleton, like grasshoppers and cicadas, grow in steps (intermittent growth). Vertebrates like cattle, goats and humans grow continuously, giving an S-shaped curve. Hormones control the process. Brain hormone (PTTH) triggers ecdysone to cause moulting, and juvenile hormone (JH) decides whether the insect stays a larva or nymph or changes into an adult. Insects with complete metamorphosis, like butterflies, change shape totally because JH drops, while those with incomplete metamorphosis, like grasshoppers, look like small adults all along.

sections.title: 2. Evidence: Growth Patterns and the Exuvia
sections.prompt: Describe the evidence from the empty exuvia and from growth curves. Compare the graph of an insect (such as a grasshopper nymph in Nairobi or Kisumu) with the graph of a vertebrate (such as a calf or a child). Explain what the shape of each graph shows.
sections.exemplar: The exuvia we found on the maize leaf was crunchy, perfectly shaped and split down the back. Next to it was a grasshopper clearly larger than the shell. This shows the shell was left behind and the animal grew bigger than it, so the insect did not peel like sunburned skin. It left through the split. When we plotted body size against time for a grasshopper, the graph looked like a staircase: size stayed flat while the hard shell was in place, then jumped up at each moult. This is intermittent growth. When we plotted a vertebrate such as a calf or a child, the graph was a smooth S-shaped (sigmoid) curve with four phases: a lag phase where growth is slow, an exponential phase where growth is rapid, a deceleration phase where growth slows down, and a stationary phase where size stays steady in the adult. A vertebrate has an internal skeleton that grows with the body, so no shell must be shed.

sections.title: 3. Evidence: Types of Metamorphosis
sections.prompt: Use photos or samples of a butterfly life cycle and a grasshopper life cycle. Describe the stages of complete and incomplete metamorphosis and explain how the caterpillar-to-butterfly change is different from a grasshopper's growth.
sections.exemplar: A butterfly (for example, the common African monarch seen in Kericho tea farms) goes through complete metamorphosis: egg, larva (caterpillar), pupa, adult. The caterpillar looks nothing like the adult. It eats leaves and moults several times, then becomes a motionless pupa. Inside, the body is reorganised under hormone control into wings and adult organs, so it does not simply melt and rebuild at random. A grasshopper goes through incomplete metamorphosis: egg, nymph, adult. The nymph looks like a small adult without full wings and grows through several moults until it is an adult. There is no pupa stage. So both groups moult, but only the butterfly has a pupa stage and a completely different body shape in the adult.

sections.title: 4. Reasoning: Hormonal Control of Moulting and Metamorphosis
sections.prompt: Explain step by step how the hormones PTTH, ecdysone and juvenile hormone control moulting and metamorphosis. Link this reasoning back to your claim and evidence and to the exuvia and the pupa.
sections.exemplar: Moulting is controlled by a chain of hormones. First, the brain releases Brain Hormone (PTTH). PTTH stimulates the prothoracic glands to release ecdysone. Ecdysone triggers the insect to moult, which is why the exuvia splits and the animal climbs out larger. Juvenile hormone (JH) decides what kind of moult happens. When JH concentration is high, ecdysone causes a moult that keeps the larval or nymph form, so the caterpillar or nymph just gets bigger. When JH decreases, ecdysone causes pupation and then metamorphosis into the adult. This explains our evidence: the staircase graph shows moults caused by ecdysone, the grasshopper stays similar in shape because JH is present through the nymph stages, and the butterfly changes shape completely because JH falls so the caterpillar becomes a pupa and then an adult. So the changes are controlled by hormones and are not random melting.

sections.title: 5. Annotated Graphical Model and Conclusion
sections.prompt: Describe the annotated model you would draw on your poster. Include both growth curves, the hormone sequence, and labels for the exuvia and the life cycles. Finish with a conclusion that answers the driving question and corrects one misconception.
sections.exemplar: My poster model has two graphs side by side. On the left is a staircase graph labelled 'Insect: intermittent growth' with arrows at each step marked 'ecdysis: ecdysone peak, old exuvia shed'. On the right is an S-shaped curve labelled 'Vertebrate: continuous growth' with the lag, exponential, deceleration and stationary phases marked. Below the graphs is a flow diagram: Brain, PTTH, prothoracic glands, ecdysone, moult. Beside it is a box: 'High JH = stay larva/nymph; low JH = pupate and become adult'. I draw a butterfly cycle (egg, larva, pupa, adult) and a grasshopper cycle (egg, nymph, adult) with a photo of the exuvia from the school garden. My conclusion: An insect outgrows its hard shell by moulting in steps controlled by ecdysone, and juvenile hormone decides whether it only grows bigger or changes shape completely. A common misconception is that insects peel like skin or melt without control, but actually the exoskeleton is shed whole and every change is hormone-controlled.

rubric.excellent: The claim fully answers both parts of the driving question, names both growth patterns, and mentions the role of hormones in clear language.
rubric.proficient: The claim answers the driving question but leaves out one idea, such as the hormones or one growth pattern.
rubric.developing: The claim is vague, incomplete, or only partly related to the driving question.

rubric.excellent: Uses specific evidence from the exuvia, the staircase and S-shaped graphs, and the life cycles, with accurate details such as the growth phases and the pupa stage.
rubric.proficient: Uses relevant evidence from most sources but some details are general or missing.
rubric.developing: Evidence is limited, inaccurate, or not linked to the phenomenon.

rubric.excellent: Correctly explains the sequence of PTTH, prothoracic glands, ecdysone and the role of high versus low juvenile hormone, and links it clearly to the claim and evidence.
rubric.proficient: Explains most of the hormone sequence with a small error or a weak link to the evidence.
rubric.developing: Hormone roles are missing, confused, or listed without explanation.

rubric.excellent: Model is accurate, fully labelled, and shows both growth curves, the four sigmoid phases, the hormone sequence, and both types of metamorphosis.
rubric.proficient: Model includes most required parts with a few missing labels or small errors.
rubric.developing: Model is incomplete, unclear, or contains major errors.

rubric.excellent: Writing is clear and well organised, uses scientific terms correctly (ecdysis, exuvia, metamorphosis), uses Kenyan contexts, and corrects a misconception.
rubric.proficient: Writing is mostly clear and uses most terms correctly, with limited local context or no misconception addressed.
rubric.developing: Writing is hard to follow, and scientific terms are missing or misused.

SUMMARY_TABLE.subStrand: Sub-Strand 3.2: Growth and Development in Animals
SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: DRIVING QUESTION: How does an animal outgrow its own hard shell, and why do some animals radically change shape while others just grow bigger?

lessons.title: The Empty Skin on the Maize Leaf: Two Ways Insects Grow
lessons.observed: Learners examine real or pictured specimens from a Kenyan maize field: an empty grasshopper skin (exuvia) on a leaf, grasshopper nymphs of different sizes, and the life stages of a butterfly or the maize stalk borer (egg, larva, pupa, adult). Teacher note: use WAIT TIME of 10 seconds after asking 'What do you think the empty skin is?' and cold-call 3 learners to share predictions before revealing the answer. Learners notice that grasshopper nymphs look like small adults, whereas caterpillars and maggots look nothing like the adult.
lessons.learned: Insects follow two developmental pathways. Incomplete metamorphosis (egg, nymph, adult: 3 stages), as in the grasshopper, has nymphs that resemble small wingless adults and grow through successive moults. Complete metamorphosis (egg, larva, pupa, adult: 4 stages), as in the butterfly, housefly and maize stalk borer, has a larva that looks totally different from the adult, and a pupa stage in which the body is reorganised. Teacher note: stress that the empty skin is the shed exoskeleton, evidence that the insect grew by moulting.
lessons.explained: The empty skin on the maize leaf is the cast-off exoskeleton left when a grasshopper nymph moulted and grew larger. Model answer: a grasshopper grows by shedding its skin several times, and each nymph stage looks like a smaller adult (incomplete metamorphosis), while a butterfly or stalk borer changes shape radically through larva and pupa stages (complete metamorphosis). Common misconception to correct: the empty skin is not a dead insect. Add the first questions to the DQB: 'Why must the insect shed its skin?' and 'Why does a caterpillar not look like a butterfly?'

lessons.title: Stepwise Growth: Why Hard-Shelled Animals Grow in Jumps
lessons.observed: Learners study a table or graph of body length of a grasshopper nymph (or a crab from the Mombasa coast) measured over several weeks, and plot size against time. They see flat periods when the size stays the same, followed by sudden jumps. Teacher note: ask learners to 'describe the shape of the graph' before interpreting it, allow 10 seconds of WAIT TIME, and cold-call 3 learners. A simple model with a tight-fitting paper sleeve or a non-stretching glove helps show why a rigid covering limits growth.
lessons.learned: Animals with a hard exoskeleton cannot grow smoothly because the shell does not stretch. They must moult (ecdysis) first: the old cuticle is shed, then the animal swells by taking in air or water while the new cuticle is still soft, and then the new cuticle hardens (sclerotisation). Growth therefore happens in jumps (a stepwise growth curve), with the periods between moults, called instars, showing almost no increase in size. Teacher note: emphasise that tissue growth can occur inside, but external size increases only at moulting.
lessons.explained: Model answer to the driving question: an insect outgrows its hard shell by moulting, shedding the old exoskeleton, expanding quickly while the new one is soft, then hardening it. This produces a staircase growth curve rather than a smooth one. Vulnerability point: a freshly moulted insect is soft and exposed to predators such as birds, so moulting is risky. Update the DQB with: 'What tells the insect when to moult?' Learners add the stepwise curve to the class model.

lessons.title: Growth Curves: Why Do Vertebrates and Soft-Bodied Animals Grow Smoothly in an S-Shape While Insects with Hard Shells Grow in Steps?
lessons.observed: Learners plot and compare data sets: the mass of a Kenyan Boran calf or a human child (or tilapia from Lake Victoria fish ponds) over time, and the stepwise length of an insect nymph. Teacher note: give learners graph paper, let them plot individually for 5 minutes, then compare in pairs. They should observe that the vertebrate curve is a smooth S-shape while the insect curve is stepped. Ask: 'Where is growth fastest? Where does it slow down?' and allow WAIT TIME before cold-calling 3 learners.
lessons.learned: Vertebrates and soft-bodied animals grow continuously in a sigmoid (S-shaped) curve with four phases: lag (slow start while the organism adapts), exponential or log (rapid growth), deceleration (growth slows as limits such as food and space are reached) and stationary (growth levels off). Growth rate = (final size − initial size) ÷ time taken. Teacher note: work a calculation, for example a calf growing from 30 kg to 150 kg in 6 months gives (150 − 30) ÷ 6 = 20 kg per month. Insects with a rigid exoskeleton show a stepped curve, although their overall trend over time is still roughly sigmoid.
lessons.explained: Model answer: vertebrates have an internal skeleton (endoskeleton) that grows with the body, so they increase in size continuously and give a smooth S-curve. Insects have an external skeleton that cannot stretch, so their size increases only at moulting, giving a staircase curve. Learners should be able to label the four phases and calculate growth rate correctly with units. Common error: confusing the stationary phase with death. Add to the DQB: 'What controls the timing of the steps?' and revise the model to show both curve types.

lessons.title: Hormones as the Control Switches of Moulting and Metamorphosis
lessons.observed: Learners study a flow diagram and data from classic experiments (for example Wigglesworth's work on the blood-sucking bug Rhodnius, where decapitation at different times affected moulting) and discuss what happens when the head, brain or glands are removed or hormones are injected. Teacher note: use a 'think-pair-share' with 10 seconds of WAIT TIME and cold-call 3 pairs to state the cause-and-effect chain. Ask: 'What does the evidence tell us about where the moulting signal comes from?'
lessons.learned: Brain Hormone (from neurosecretory cells in the brain) signals the prothoracic glands to release Ecdysone, which triggers moulting. Juvenile Hormone (JH), from the corpora allata, decides the kind of moult: high levels keep the insect juvenile (the moult gives another nymph or larva), while falling levels allow the next stage to develop towards the pupa and adult. Teacher note: Ecdysone says 'moult now'; JH says 'what to become'. Sequence: brain → Brain Hormone → prothoracic glands → Ecdysone → moult.
lessons.explained: Model answer: moulting is not random but under hormonal control, with Brain Hormone acting as the first switch, Ecdysone as the moulting trigger and Juvenile Hormone as the decision-maker for the type of moult. This answers the DQB question 'What tells the insect when to moult?' Learners should state that endocrine control ensures growth stages happen in the correct order and timing. Add the hormone pathway to the class model and pose a new DQB question: 'How does JH decide between staying young and becoming an adult?'

lessons.title: The Chemical Switch: How Juvenile Hormone Decides Whether an Insect Stays Young or Becomes an Adult
lessons.observed: Learners analyse data tables or diagrams showing JH levels at each moult in an insect, and results of experiments in which extra JH is applied to a larva or JH-producing glands are removed. They observe that extra JH produces an extra larval stage or giant larvae, while removing the glands leads to premature pupation or tiny adults. Teacher note: ask learners to predict before revealing results, allow 10 seconds of WAIT TIME, and cold-call 3 learners to justify their predictions with evidence.
lessons.learned: Moulting is triggered by ecdysone, and the level of Juvenile Hormone decides what type of moult occurs: high JH means the insect moults into another nymph or larva (stays juvenile); low JH means it moults into a pupa (in complete metamorphosis) or directly into an adult (in incomplete metamorphosis); no JH at the last moult gives the adult. Teacher note: use the analogy of a 'stay young' dial. Application: JH-mimicking insecticides can stop pests such as mosquitoes from becoming adults, and farmers can use this in integrated pest management.
lessons.explained: Model answer: the same ecdysone signal produces different results depending on the JH level, so JH acts as the chemical switch between staying young and becoming an adult. This explains why a caterpillar grows through several larval moults before pupating. Check understanding with the question: 'What would happen if a locust nymph were given extra JH?' Expected answer: it would stay in a nymph stage and delay becoming an adult. Update the DQB and the model with the JH decision step.

lessons.title: Final Explanation: Controlled Growth, Metamorphosis and Survival in Kenyan Insects
lessons.observed: Learners revisit the anchoring phenomenon (the empty skin on the maize leaf) and review their DQB, stepwise graphs and hormone model. They apply their understanding to Kenyan insects such as the desert locust (incomplete), the maize stalk borer, the silkworm and the mosquito (complete), and consider survival advantages. Teacher note: allow WAIT TIME of 10 seconds after each prompt, cold-call 3 learners per question, and have learners present gallery-walk models using evidence from all lessons.
lessons.learned: An insect's hard exoskeleton cannot stretch, so the insect moults (ecdysis) under hormone control: ecdysone triggers moulting and juvenile hormone decides whether the next stage is another juvenile or an adult. Incomplete metamorphosis (egg, nymph, adult) gives gradual change, while complete metamorphosis (egg, larva, pupa, adult) gives radical change. Complete metamorphosis reduces competition because larvae and adults use different foods and habitats (for example, caterpillars eat leaves while adult butterflies drink nectar). Vertebrates grow continuously in an S-shaped curve because their skeleton is internal.
lessons.explained: Model answer to the driving question: an animal outgrows its hard shell by moulting, shedding the old exoskeleton and expanding before the new one hardens, with growth in steps controlled by ecdysone and JH. Some animals radically change shape (complete metamorphosis) because JH levels fall to allow a pupal stage and adult reorganisation, with survival benefits such as less competition between young and adults, while others, such as grasshoppers and vertebrates, simply grow bigger. Assess using the final model: look for correct use of ecdysis, ecdysone, JH, instars, the stepped versus S-shaped curves and a Kenyan example. Common misconception to resolve: hormones do not make the shell grow; they trigger and direct moulting. Close by resolving the DQB questions, marking each as answered.
